facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mendeleev was so confident in his periodic pattern that he correctly predicted the density and melting points of missing elements.

facts_and_myths.claim: Chemical reactions in laboratories always result in dramatic, bubbling, colorful explosions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The vast majority of chemistry reactions produce subtle clear solutions, slight color shifts, or microscopic crystalline precipitates.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Uncontrolled explosions represent dangerous laboratory procedural accidents rather than normal scientific experiments.

name: Geneticist
visual_anchor: A molecular geneticist in purple nitrile gloves holding a glowing fluorescent agarose electrophoresis gel slab revealing distinct ultraviolet DNA banding lines.
core_traits: Studies the molecular mechanisms of heredity, gene expression, and DNA/RNA sequence variation
Performs polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification, gel electrophoresis, and next-generation sequencing
Utilizes CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technologies to modify precise gene sequences
Identifies genetic mutations responsible for congenital syndromes and hereditary diseases

facts_and_myths.claim: If uncoiled and laid end to end, the DNA inside a single human cell would measure roughly two meters long.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cellular DNA is extraordinarily tightly wound and packaged around histone proteins to fit inside a microscopic nucleus only six microns wide.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The total DNA in all cells of a human body stretched end to end would reach to Pluto and back multiple times.

facts_and_myths.claim: Gregor Mendel founded the foundational laws of genetics in the 1860s by breeding laboratory mice.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mendel was an Austrian monk who conducted his groundbreaking heredity experiments using thousands of common pea plants in a monastery garden.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: His work on dominant and recessive traits was largely ignored by the scientific community until decades after his death.

name: Oceanographer
visual_anchor: An oceanographer on the aft deck of an oceanographic research vessel deploying a massive circular CTD rosette instrument carousel into churning blue open ocean waters.
core_traits: Studies the physical, chemical, and geological dynamics of global oceans and deep abyssal plains
Deploys autonomous underwater gliders, deep-sea benthic landers, and CTD sensors (conductivity, temperature, depth)
Maps the global thermohaline ocean conveyor belt and deep underwater mid-ocean ridge systems
Investigates seafloor hydrothermal vents, tectonic subduction trenches, and ocean circulation models

facts_and_myths.claim: The largest mountain range on Earth is located entirely underwater beneath the ocean.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Mid-Ocean Ridge system stretches over 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles) across every ocean basin, dwarfing the Andes and Himalayas.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It was discovered and mapped in detail by oceanographer Marie Tharp using sonar depth profiles in the 1950s.

facts_and_myths.claim: Oceanographers and marine biologists do the exact same job with the same academic credentials.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Marine biologists study living ocean organisms, whereas physical and geological oceanographers study currents, tides, water chemistry, and seabed tectonics.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Physical oceanographers frequently hold advanced degrees in applied mathematics and geophysical fluid dynamics.

name: Seismologist
visual_anchor: A seismologist analyzing jagged digital drum seismograms showing primary and secondary earthquake arrival waves across global monitoring stations.
core_traits: Geophysicist who studies the origin, propagation, and effects of earthquakes and mechanical elastic waves through Earth
Analyzes P-waves (primary compressional) and S-waves (secondary shear) on digital broadband seismometers
Locates earthquake epicenters, focal depths, and faults using seismic triangulation networks
Investigates the internal concentric structure of Earth's crust, mantle, liquid outer core, and solid inner core

facts_and_myths.claim: The Richter earthquake magnitude scale increases linearly, where magnitude 6 is just slightly stronger than magnitude 5.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Richter and Moment Magnitude scales are logarithmic; each whole unit represents roughly 32 times more released energy.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A magnitude 7 earthquake releases roughly 1,000 times more seismic energy than a magnitude 5 earthquake.

facts_and_myths.claim: Scientists deduced that Earth has a liquid outer core because seismic shear waves (S-waves) cannot travel through liquids.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Seismologist Inge Lehmann and Richard Oldham observed that S-waves cast a distinct 'shadow zone' where they are blocked by liquid iron.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lehmann subsequently discovered that Earth also contains a solid inner core nestled inside that liquid outer shell.

name: Glaciologist
visual_anchor: A glaciologist in a red polar parka and glacier crampons extracting a transparent cylindrical ice core cylinder with a motorized drill on an Antarctic ice sheet.
core_traits: Scientist who studies natural ice formations, alpine glaciers, continental ice caps, and polar ice shelves
Drills deep polar ice cores that trap ancient atmospheric air bubbles dating back hundreds of thousands of years
Measures glacial velocity, crevasse propagation, and mass balance using satellite laser altimetry and GPS stakes
Monitors sea level rise risks resulting from the melting of Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets

facts_and_myths.claim: Glacier ice looks distinctly vibrant blue because it contains frozen blue mineral dust.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Glacier ice appears blue because immense pressure squeezes out air bubbles; dense crystalline ice absorbs red light and reflects blue light.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The older and more compressed glacial ice becomes, the deeper and more vivid its sapphire-blue hue.

facts_and_myths.claim: Antarctic ice core samples provide continuous records of Earth's atmospheric greenhouse gases spanning over 800,000 years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tiny atmospheric gas bubbles trapped between compacted snow grains act as pristine time capsules of ancient air.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Glaciologists can determine prehistoric global temperatures by measuring oxygen and hydrogen isotope ratios in the ice.

name: Astrobiologist
visual_anchor: An astrobiologist collecting extremophile microbial mats from an acidic boiling geothermal spring in Yellowstone to simulate potential life on Mars.
core_traits: Studies the origins, evolution, distribution, and future of life in the universe
Investigates terrestrial extremophiles living in boiling hydrothermal pools, radioactive mines, and subglacial lakes
Designs biosignature detection instruments for robotic rovers exploring Mars and icy ocean moons like Europa and Enceladus
Examines meteorites for prebiotic organic molecules, amino acids, and chemical biosignatures

facts_and_myths.claim: Tardigrades (water bears) can survive the freezing vacuum and intense radiation of outer space.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 2007, the European Space Agency launched desiccated tardigrades into low Earth orbit for 10 days, and many survived and reproduced upon rehydration.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tardigrades enter an almost indestructible cryptobiotic state called a 'tun' by replacing cell water with protective proteins.

facts_and_myths.claim: Astrobiologists have already confirmed the discovery of living intelligent extraterrestrial civilizations.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While prebiotic organic molecules and thousands of exoplanets have been discovered, confirmed alien life has not yet been found.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The field primarily focuses on identifying potential microbial signatures in extraterrestrial subsurface oceans.

name: Entomologist
visual_anchor: An entomologist using fine forceps to examine the iridescent compound eyes of a pinned tropical beetle specimen under a stereo zoom laboratory microscope.
core_traits: Biological scientist who specializes in the study of insects, their physiology, behavior, and ecology
Collects specimens using sweep nets, light traps, and aspirators, cataloging species in pinned entomological drawers
Researches insect pollination ecology, agricultural pest biological controls, and vector-borne diseases like malaria
Studies social insect superorganisms like ants, termites, and honeybee colonies

facts_and_myths.claim: Insects make up more than 50% of all known living organism species on the entire planet.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Over one million distinct insect species have been cataloged by scientists, with estimates suggesting millions more remain undiscovered.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Beetles (order Coleoptera) alone represent about 25% of all known animal species on Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: All crawling bugs, spiders, centipedes, and scorpions are technically classified as true insects.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Insects strictly possess three body segments (head, thorax, abdomen) and six legs; spiders and scorpions are eight-legged arachnids.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Centipedes are myriapods with many legs, and pillbugs are terrestrial crustaceans related to lobsters.

name: Anthropologist
visual_anchor: An anthropologist taking field notes in a leather journal while observing cultural ceremonial rituals in a remote highland village community.
core_traits: Scientist who studies human biology, evolutionary origins, linguistics, cultures, and societal development
Conducts ethnographic participant observation, immersion fieldwork, and oral history interviews
Analyzes fossilized hominin skeletal remains like Australopithecus and Neanderthals
Explores comparative cultural customs, kinship structures, folklore, and ritual traditions

facts_and_myths.claim: Neanderthals were unintelligent, hunched brutes completely distinct and isolated from modern Homo sapiens.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Neanderthals used fire, created symbolic art, buried their dead, and interbred with Homo sapiens; non-African modern humans carry 1-2% Neanderthal DNA.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Neanderthal cranial brain volumes were actually slightly larger on average than modern human brains.

facts_and_myths.claim: The famous 3.2-million-year-old hominin fossil 'Lucy' was named after a Beatles song playing in the expedition camp.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Paleoanthropologist Donald Johanson and his team celebrated discovering the Australopithecus skeleton in Ethiopia while listening to 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lucy walked upright on two feet, proving bipedalism evolved before large brain expansion in early human ancestors.

name: Robotics Engineer
visual_anchor: A robotics engineer in a tech lab calibrating a multi-jointed industrial robotic arm using a wireless tablet controller next to a prototype quadruped robot.
core_traits: Designs, builds, programs, and maintains autonomous robots and robotic automated systems
Integrates mechanical components, microcontrollers, servo motors, LiDAR sensors, and computer vision cameras
Writes motion control algorithms, inverse kinematics calculations, and SLAM navigation routines
Develops automated manufacturing cells, surgical robots, warehouse autonomous rovers, and planetary probes

facts_and_myths.claim: The word 'robot' was coined in 1920 by Czech writer Karel Capek in a theatrical play about artificial workers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Derived from the Slavic word 'robota', meaning forced labor or servitude, introduced in Capek's play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Isaac Asimov later coined the term 'robotics' and formulated the famous fictional Three Laws of Robotics.

facts_and_myths.claim: All modern autonomous robots possess sentient human-like emotional consciousness and self-awareness.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Robots execute deterministic mathematics, sensor feedback loops, and machine learning models without subjective emotional consciousness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Even the most lifelike humanoid robots are advanced electro-mechanical machines running pre-programmed algorithms.

name: Aerospace Engineer
visual_anchor: An aerospace engineer examining aerodynamic airflow streamlines around a scale prototype rocket model inside a massive supersonic wind tunnel test facility.
core_traits: Designs, analyzes, and tests aircraft, spacecraft, satellites, and rocket propulsion systems
Calculates aerodynamic lift-to-drag ratios, supersonic shockwaves, and orbital trajectory burns
Utilizes computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, finite element structural analysis, and wind tunnels
Engineers lightweight composite airframes, turbofan jet engines, and rocket combustion chambers

facts_and_myths.claim: Airplanes fly because air travels faster over the curved top of the wing to reach the trailing edge at the same time as air below.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The 'equal transit time' theory is false; wings generate lift by deflecting a mass of air downward (Newton's 3rd law) and creating a low-pressure vortex.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Air flowing over the top of a wing actually reaches the trailing edge significantly earlier than air moving underneath.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rocket engines operate more efficiently in the absolute vacuum of space than they do within Earth's atmosphere.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In space, there is zero atmospheric backpressure fighting the expanding rocket exhaust, allowing gases to expand at maximum exit velocity.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Rockets carry both liquid fuel and liquid oxidizer tanks because there is no ambient oxygen in space to burn.

name: Software Developer
visual_anchor: A software engineer with dual widescreen monitors displaying dark-themed syntax-highlighted code and terminal windows typing on a mechanical keyboard.
core_traits: Designs, writes, tests, and deploys computer software applications, operating systems, and web services
Codes in modern programming languages like Python, TypeScript, Rust, C++, and Go
Implements data structures, algorithms, automated unit tests, and version control via Git
Collaborates across software architectures using continuous integration, microservices, and cloud deployments

facts_and_myths.claim: Ada Lovelace wrote the world's first published machine algorithm in 1843, becoming the first computer programmer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lovelace wrote an algorithm for Charles Babbage's mechanical Analytical Engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, foreseeing that computers could manipulate symbols beyond numbers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The early programming language 'Ada' was officially named by the U.S. Department of Defense in her honor.

facts_and_myths.claim: Software developers spend their entire workday writing uninterrupted code at 100 words per minute without debugging.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Developers spend the majority of their time reading existing code, designing architectures, debugging edge cases, and reading technical documentation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Finding and fixing a single subtle logic bug or off-by-one error can sometimes take days of deep troubleshooting.

name: Cybersecurity Analyst
visual_anchor: A cybersecurity analyst in a security operations center (SOC) tracking real-time global cyberattack vectors across an illuminated world map video wall.
core_traits: Monitors networks, servers, and cloud environments to detect, analyze, and neutralize cyber intrusions
Conducts vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and ethical hacking exercises
Configures firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS), zero-trust access, and encryption protocols
Performs digital forensics on malware infections, ransomware payloads, and data breaches

facts_and_myths.claim: Real hackers bypass enterprise encryption by typing rapidly with green falling matrix code on dark screens in 10 seconds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hollywood cinematic hacking is purely theatrical; real cyber attacks take months of patient reconnaissance, social engineering, and misconfigured credential exploitation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 80% of successful enterprise data breaches begin with human-targeted phishing emails rather than complex zero-day coding exploits.

facts_and_myths.claim: The word 'bug' in computing was popularized when a real moth was discovered stuck inside a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Computer pioneer Grace Hopper and her team taped the moth into their logbook with the entry: 'First actual case of bug being found.'
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: That original taped moth logbook page is preserved today in the Smithsonian National Museum of American History.

name: Civil Engineer
visual_anchor: A civil engineer wearing a white hard hat and high-vis safety vest reviewing architectural bridge blueprints on a tripod table overlooking a suspension bridge construction site.
core_traits: Plans, designs, and oversees construction of public infrastructure: bridges, highways, dams, tunnels, and water systems
Calculates structural load distribution, soil mechanics, concrete tensile strength, and seismic resistance
Utilizes CAD modeling, topographic surveys, environmental impact reports, and building code specifications
Ensures massive structures endure extreme wind loads, thermal expansion, and century-level floods

facts_and_myths.claim: Long suspension bridges are engineered to sway several feet horizontally in strong gales without collapsing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Flexibility prevents catastrophic harmonic fracture; aerodynamic deck profiles and tuned mass dampers dissipate immense kinetic wind energy safely.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Golden Gate Bridge can sway up to 27 feet sideways and move 10 feet up and down during severe storms.

facts_and_myths.claim: Civil engineers and architects perform identical tasks and require the exact same training license.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Architects focus primarily on aesthetic form, spatial functionality, and user experience, while Civil Engineers calculate physics, loads, materials, and structural safety.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Architects design how a building looks and feels; civil engineers ensure the building will not physically collapse.

name: Mechanical Engineer
visual_anchor: A mechanical engineer in an engineering workshop testing a high-precision titanium gearbox assembly using digital vernier calipers and 3D CAD models.
core_traits: Designs, develops, and tests mechanical machines, thermal energy devices, engines, and automated mechanisms
Applies principles of thermodynamics, kinematics, material mechanics, and heat transfer
Models mechanical assemblies using 3D CAD software and performs stress finite element analysis (FEA)
Develops internal combustion engines, HVAC systems, industrial turbines, and consumer appliances

facts_and_myths.claim: Perpetual motion machines that produce continuous free energy forever are mathematically and physically impossible.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The first and second laws of thermodynamics strictly dictate that energy cannot be created from nothing and entropy always increases through friction.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Patent offices worldwide automatically reject patent applications for perpetual motion machines unless a working physical prototype is presented.

facts_and_myths.claim: Mechanical engineers only work on repairing broken car engines with hand wrenches like auto mechanics.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mechanical engineers design the underlying physics and manufactured parts for power plants, aerospace crafts, medical implants, and micro-electromechanical sensors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mechanical engineering is one of the broadest and oldest engineering disciplines in human history.

name: Electrical Engineer
visual_anchor: An electrical engineer probing a multi-layer printed circuit board (PCB) with an oscilloscope test probe beneath bright magnifying bench lights.
core_traits: Designs, tests, and oversees the manufacture of electrical systems, circuits, microchips, and power generation grids
Analyzes circuit signals using digital oscilloscopes, spectrum analyzers, and multimeter instruments
Designs high-voltage transmission grids, transformers, electric vehicle powertrains, and integrated circuits
Applies electromagnetism, circuit theory, signal processing, and semiconductor physics

facts_and_myths.claim: Electricity flows through electrical wires at exactly the speed of light.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Individual electrons drift through copper wires at a few millimeters per second; it is the electromagnetic wave energy that travels down the wire at near light speed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The drift velocity of an electron in a typical household wire is slower than a walking snail.

facts_and_myths.claim: The fierce 'War of the Currents' between Thomas Edison's DC and Nikola Tesla's AC was won by AC for power transmission.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Alternating Current (AC) can be easily stepped up to high voltages with transformers, allowing electrical power to travel hundreds of miles with minimal heat loss.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tesla teamed up with George Westinghouse to build the first major AC hydroelectric power plant at Niagara Falls in 1895.

name: Electrician
visual_anchor: A skilled electrician with a leather tool belt testing voltage on a complex circuit breaker panel with insulated wire strippers and a digital multimeter.
core_traits: Installs, connects, tests, and repairs electrical wiring, conduits, circuit breakers, and lighting fixtures
Follows rigorous National Electrical Code (NEC) standards and blueprint wiring schematics
Uses specialized insulated hand tools, fish tapes, conduit benders, and digital voltage testers
Diagnoses electrical faults, short circuits, tripped breakers, and grounding hazards

facts_and_myths.claim: Pure distilled water is an exceptional conductor of dangerous household electricity.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Completely pure deionized water is actually an insulator; it is dissolved minerals and salt ions in tap water that conduct electric currents.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: However, even tiny traces of sweat or dust provide enough ions to make water highly conductive and hazardous.

facts_and_myths.claim: Birds can sit harmlessly on bare high-voltage power lines because they do not complete an electrical circuit to the ground.
facts_and_myths.explanation: With both feet on the same wire, there is no voltage potential difference across the bird's body, so electricity stays on the lower-resistance copper line.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If a large bird touches two separate wires or a wire and a grounded utility pole simultaneously, it suffers a fatal shock.

name: Plumber
visual_anchor: An experienced plumber in work overalls tightening a heavy pipe wrench around a copper water pipe joint under a residential basement sink.
core_traits: Installs, inspects, and repairs water supply networks, drainage systems, gas lines, and waste disposal fixtures
Solders copper pipe joints with propane torches and connects PVC, PEX, and cast-iron pipelines
Clears blocked sewer lines using motorized drain snakes, hydro-jetters, and sewer inspection cameras
Ensures municipal sanitation standards and installs backflow preventers to protect drinking water

facts_and_myths.claim: Pouring boiling hot water down kitchen drains clears heavy grease clogs permanently.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Boiling water merely melts grease and carries it a few feet deeper into cooler underground pipes where it congeals into stubborn solid fatbergs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Plumbers recommend wiping grease into trash cans with paper towels rather than washing it down any drain.

facts_and_myths.claim: The word 'plumber' comes from the Latin word 'plumbum', which means lead.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Ancient Romans constructed their monumental city aqueducts and municipal bath pipes using malleable lead metal.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The chemical symbol for lead on the Periodic Table is still 'Pb' from the Latin root plumbum.

name: Carpenter
visual_anchor: A master carpenter in a heavy canvas apron smoothing a rich walnut tabletop with a wooden hand plane, fine wood shavings curling around the workbench.
core_traits: Cuts, shapes, and joins timber and wooden building materials to construct furniture, cabinetry, and structural frames
Uses hand tools and power tools including chisels, hand planes, miter saws, routers, and claw hammers
Masters joinery techniques such as dovetails, mortise and tenon, lap joints, and dowel pinning
Interprets architectural blueprints, calculates framing angles, and applies protective finishes

facts_and_myths.claim: Ancient traditional Japanese pagodas were built entirely of wood without using a single metal nail or screw.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Master Japanese carpenters invented intricate interlocking wood joints (kigumi) that absorb earthquake ground tremors through friction.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Horyu-ji temple in Japan has stood for over 1,300 years, making it one of the oldest wooden buildings on Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: Hardwoods are always physically harder and denser than softwoods without exception.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hardwood and softwood are botanical classifications based on tree reproduction; balsa wood is botanically a hardwood yet is softer than almost all softwoods.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Yew wood is botanically a softwood (gymnosperm) but is significantly harder than many common hardwoods.

name: Blacksmith
visual_anchor: A muscular blacksmith in a heavy leather apron hammering a glowing cherry-red steel billet on a heavy steel anvil, showering golden sparks across a dark forge workshop.
core_traits: Forges wrought iron and steel by heating metal in a coal or gas forge and shaping it with hammers and anvils
Masters traditional metalworking techniques: drawing out, upsetting, bending, punching, and forge-welding
Controls steel temper through thermal heat-treatment, oil quenching, and color-judged annealing
Crafts architectural ironwork, custom cutlery, forged tools, hinges, and historic replicas

facts_and_myths.claim: Blacksmiths judge the precise internal temperature of glowing hot steel by its visual radiation color.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Steel glows from faint dull red (1,000 degrees F) to cherry red, bright orange, and blinding white-hot (2,400 degrees F) as its thermal energy increases.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Traditional smiths keep forges dimly lit so they can accurately discern subtle color variations in hot steel.

facts_and_myths.claim: Quenching red-hot steel in cold water makes the blade immediately flexible and ready for heavy chopping.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Immediate water quenching transforms steel into martensite, which is glass-brittle and will shatter if struck; it must be carefully tempered with gentle heat.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tempering relieves internal stress and restores toughness to the hardened steel.

name: Welder
visual_anchor: A welder wearing an auto-darkening welding helmet and leather gauntlets laying a flawless bead of TIG weld on a stainless steel pipe, creating a brilliant blue-white electric arc.
core_traits: Fuses metal pieces together using intense electrical arcs or gas torches to melt base metals and filler rod
Proficient in diverse welding processes: SMAW (Stick), GMAW (MIG), GTAW (TIG), and flux-cored welding
Wears specialized protective equipment: dark auto-darkening shade helmets, leather jackets, and respirators
Produces certified structural welds on skyscrapers, pressure vessels, pipelines, and ship hulls

facts_and_myths.claim: The temperature of an electric welding arc can exceed 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit, hotter than the surface of the Sun.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Concentrated electrical plasma arcs reach temperatures between 6,000 degrees F and 20,000 degrees F, melting structural metals in a fraction of a second.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The surface of the Sun is roughly 10,000 degrees F, meaning a welding arc is comparable in thermal intensity.

facts_and_myths.claim: Looking at a welding arc without a shield only causes mild temporary tearing with no permanent risk.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Welding arcs emit intense ultraviolet radiation that causes 'arc eye' (photokeratitis) - a painful corneal sunburn - and permanent retinal burns.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Arc eye feels like your eyeballs have been coated in coarse sand and lasts for days.

name: Construction Worker
visual_anchor: A determined construction worker in a high-visibility yellow vest, yellow hard hat, and steel-toe boots carrying heavy rebar across an active skyscraper foundation site.
core_traits: Performs essential physical labor and structural tasks on building construction and civil infrastructure sites
Pours and finishes concrete, erects scaffolding, installs rebar reinforcement, and operates power equipment
Wears mandatory PPE: safety hard hats, steel-toe boots, eye protection, and high-visibility reflective vests
Works in outdoor weather extremes following strict occupational safety protocols

facts_and_myths.claim: Hard hats have been mandatory on construction projects since ancient Egyptian pyramid times.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The hard hat was invented in 1919 by Edward Dickinson Bullard; the 1930s Hoover Dam and Golden Gate Bridge were the first major projects to mandate them.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bullard based the design on the Doughboy steel helmets used by American soldiers in World War I.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cured concrete is the most widely consumed synthetic material on Earth by weight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Human civilization consumes roughly 30 billion tons of concrete annually - more than all steel, wood, plastics, and aluminum combined.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Concrete does not dry; it hardens through an exothermic chemical reaction called hydration that can continue for decades.

name: Crane Operator
visual_anchor: A focused tower crane operator sitting in a glass control cab hundreds of feet above a bustling city skyline manipulating dual joysticks to position steel beams.
core_traits: Operates massive tower cranes, crawler cranes, and mobile hydraulic cranes to lift heavy building materials
Climbs hundreds of feet up external crane vertical ladders daily to reach high-altitude cabs
Communicates with ground riggers using standardized two-way radio calls and visual hand signals
Calculates lift capacity charts, wind speed limits, load center of gravity, and boom deflection

facts_and_myths.claim: Tower cranes on skyscraper construction sites can assemble and build themselves taller as the building rises.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Using a hydraulic climbing cage section, the crane lifts a new mast section into its own midsection, jacking itself upward floor by floor.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: At the end of a project, the crane is disassembled either by a smaller derrick crane or lowered by helicopter.

facts_and_myths.claim: A crane operator can lift any weight load regardless of how far out the load sits along the horizontal boom.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Crane capacity decreases dramatically the farther the trolley travels from the mast due to the fundamental law of mechanical levers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Exceeding the load-moment indicator will cause the entire multi-ton crane to tip over or the jib boom to buckle.

name: Heavy Equipment Operator
visual_anchor: An operator in high-visibility clothing maneuvering the hydraulic joysticks of a giant yellow tracked excavator carving a massive foundation trench in raw earth.
core_traits: Operates heavy earthmoving machinery including excavators, bulldozers, backhoes, motor graders, and front loaders
Excavates foundation pits, levels subgrades, grades road beds, and clears boulders on construction sites
Controls complex hydraulic levers, foot pedals, and GPS machine-guidance elevation screens
Conducts pre-operation fluid inspections and tracks underground utility clearance markings

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern bulldozers and excavators use satellite GPS and laser guidance to grade soil automatically to millimeter accuracy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Automated machine control systems link 3D civil CAD models directly to hydraulic valves, adjusting blade heights automatically.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Operators watch real-time cab screens showing exact cut-and-fill depths down to a fraction of an inch.

facts_and_myths.claim: Hydraulic machinery utilizes compressed air gas to generate millions of pounds of digging force.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hydraulics rely on incompressible liquid mineral oil; gas compresses and cushions, whereas liquid transmits raw piston power instantly.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hydraulic oil pressures inside modern excavators can exceed 5,000 pounds per square inch (PSI).

name: Roofer
visual_anchor: A roofer wearing harness tie-offs and knee pads kneeling on a steep pitched roof nailing asphalt shingles with a pneumatic coil nail gun against an open sky.
core_traits: Installs, repairs, and replaces weatherproofing roofing systems on residential and commercial structures
Lays asphalt shingles, slate tiles, cedar shakes, standing-seam metal panels, and flat EPDM rubber membranes
Installs waterproof ice-and-water underlayment, drip edges, ridge vents, and chimney flashing
Operates safely on steep inclines using fall-arrest harnesses, roof brackets, and ladder hoists

facts_and_myths.claim: Natural slate stone roofs can survive in good condition on historic buildings for over 100 to 200 years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: High-quality metamorphic slate rock does not rot, burn, or absorb water, outlasting multiple generations of standard asphalt shingles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many medieval European cathedrals still carry their original historic slate tiles from centuries ago.

facts_and_myths.claim: Commercial 'flat roofs' are engineered completely level with zero incline or drainage pitch.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Flat roofs always have a slight mandatory slope (typically 1/4 inch per foot) directing rainwater into roof scuppers and internal drains.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A truly flat roof would allow water to pond indefinitely, causing structural collapse under immense water weight.

name: Stonemason
visual_anchor: A stonemason with stone dust on their work clothes carefully shaping a decorative granite building block with a flat chisel and wooden mallet.
core_traits: Shapes natural stone blocks and lays bricks, blocks, and ashlar masonry to build durable walls and monuments
Uses traditional hand chisels, stone pitching tools, masonry trowels, and mortar mixes
Masters dry-stone walling without mortar as well as historic lime-mortar restoration
Restores heritage stone buildings, gothic arches, stone facades, and carved gargoyles

facts_and_myths.claim: Ancient Roman concrete structures like the Pantheon remain standing after 2,000 years due to self-healing lime clasts.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Roman volcanic ash concrete containing lime clasts chemically dissolves and recrystallizes when rainwater enters cracks, self-healing fractures.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The unreinforced solid concrete dome of the Pantheon is still the largest of its kind in the world.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern mortar acts primarily as an adhesive glue that sticks heavy stones together permanently.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mortar acts as a leveling cushion that distributes compressive loads evenly across irregular stones rather than acting as a tensile glue.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In traditional masonry, the mortar must be softer than the stone so that weathering damages replaceable mortar, not the stone.

name: Locksmith
visual_anchor: A focused locksmith using a tension wrench and delicate hook pick to decode the pin tumblers inside a brass deadbolt cylinder at an illuminated workbench.
core_traits: Installs, services, rekeys, and bypasses mechanical and electronic locks, deadbolts, and high-security safes
Operates key duplicating machines, code cutters, and key blank gauges to cut precision key bittings
Understands pin tumbler mechanisms, wafer locks, tubular locks, and electronic biometric access control
Performs emergency non-destructive lock picking and safe manipulation using dial acoustics

facts_and_myths.claim: All commercial high-security bank safes can be cracked in 30 seconds with a simple stethoscope like in movies.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern combination locks have serrated wheels and false gates specifically designed to defeat acoustic listening.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Safe technicians rely on precision mathematical dialing charts, endoscopic fiber-optic borescopes, or targeted micro-drilling.

facts_and_myths.claim: Linus Yale Jr. invented the modern pin tumbler cylinder lock in the 1860s based on an ancient Egyptian wooden design.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Yale adapted an ancient 4,000-year-old Egyptian wooden pin drop mechanism into a compact brass cylinder with a small flat serrated key.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The basic pin tumbler mechanism designed by Yale remains the most widely installed door lock mechanism on Earth.

name: Auto Mechanic
visual_anchor: An auto mechanic in grease-stained coveralls inspecting a vehicle's undercarriage and brake lines with an inspection work light while the car is raised on a hydraulic two-post shop lift.
core_traits: Diagnoses, repairs, and performs routine maintenance on automobile engines, brakes, transmissions, and electrical systems
Uses computerized OBD-II diagnostic scanners, socket wrench sets, torque wrenches, and pneumatic impact guns
Replaces brake pads, timing belts, alternators, shock absorbers, and automotive fluids
Tests automotive emissions and repairs modern hybrid and electric vehicle battery packs

facts_and_myths.claim: Every car engine strictly requires an oil change every 3,000 miles without exception.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern synthetic engine oils and advanced engines reliably run between 7,500 and 10,000 miles before needing replacement.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The '3,000-mile rule' is a marketing myth left over from low-grade conventional mineral oils used in the 1960s.

facts_and_myths.claim: A modern luxury automobile contains more lines of computer software code than a Boeing 787 passenger airliner.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern vehicles contain over 100 electronic control units (ECUs) running over 100 million lines of software code for safety and engine timing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Today's auto mechanics spend as much time analyzing diagnostic data streams on computer scanners as turning mechanical wrenches.

name: Aircraft Mechanic
visual_anchor: An aircraft maintenance technician in ear protection and work uniform inspecting the titanium fan blades of a commercial jet turbofan engine inside a brightly lit hangar.
core_traits: Inspects, maintains, and repairs aircraft engines, avionics, landing gear, and flight control hydraulic systems
Holds FAA Airframe and Powerplant (A&P) certification or international aviation equivalent licensing
Performs mandatory scheduled airworthiness checks: A, B, C, and intensive structural D-checks
Signs legally binding logbook releases certifying that an aircraft is safe and airworthy for passenger flight

facts_and_myths.claim: A commercial jet aircraft can take off with known minor broken parts on its maintenance log.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Aviation authorities maintain a strictly regulated Minimum Equipment List (MEL) specifying non-critical redundant items that can defer repair.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Critical systems like flight controls and main engine components never permit deferred maintenance.

facts_and_myths.claim: A single loose metal socket wrench left inside a jet turbine will easily pass harmlessly through the exhaust.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Foreign Object Debris (FOD) can cause catastrophic blade destruction at 10,000 RPM, which is why aviation mechanics use shadowed toolboxes where every missing tool is detected immediately.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Aircraft hangars enforce strict tool inventory audits before an aircraft is allowed to exit for flight.

name: Glassblower
visual_anchor: A glassblower rotating a hollow stainless steel blowpipe with a glowing orange blob of molten glass at the mouth of a roaring 2,100-degree glory hole furnace.
core_traits: Shapes molten glass by blowing air through a long hollow blowpipe and manipulating the expanding bubble with hand tools
Operates glory hole reheaters, annealing ovens, and melt furnaces maintained above 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit
Uses traditional jacks, wooden cherry blocks, shears, and marver steel flattening tables
Crafts fine art glassware, scientific laboratory glassware, decorative vases, and stained glass

facts_and_myths.claim: Medieval church stained glass windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is a slow liquid flowing downward over centuries.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Glass is an amorphous solid that does not flow at room temperature; medieval glassmaking produced uneven sheets that builders simply installed heavy-edge down.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Optical calculations show it would take longer than the age of the universe for room-temperature glass to flow noticeably.

facts_and_myths.claim: Molten glass that cools down too quickly without annealing in a slow oven will shatter spontaneously into microscopic shards.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Annealing slowly relieves intense internal thermal stress between outer cooling layers and the hotter core of the glass object.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Famous 'Prince Rupert's drops' illustrate this stress: the bulb can withstand a hammer blow, but snipping the tail shatters the entire drop explosively.

name: Watchmaker
visual_anchor: A master watchmaker wearing an eyeglass loupe using anti-magnetic precision tweezers to seat an oscillating hairspring into a miniature mechanical watch movement.
core_traits: Crafts, assembles, regulates, and repairs complex mechanical and automatic wristwatches and pocket watches
Works with microscopic mechanical components: balance wheels, hairsprings, tourbillons, escapements, and synthetic rubies
Uses precision watchmaker lathes, staking tools, ultrasonic cleaning baths, and timing machines
Calibrates chronometer accuracy to within seconds per day against mechanical friction and gravity

facts_and_myths.claim: The tiny red 'jewels' visible inside high-end mechanical watches are purely decorative gems meant to make the watch expensive.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Watch jewels are synthetic corundum rubies used as low-friction, ultra-hard bearing surfaces that prevent steel pivot axles from wearing down.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Synthetic sapphire and ruby bearings resist wear and retain microscopic droplets of lubricating oil for years.

facts_and_myths.claim: The tourbillon mechanism was invented in 1795 by Abraham-Louis Breguet to counteract the distorting effect of Earth's gravity on pocket watches.
facts_and_myths.explanation: By mounting the balance wheel and escapement inside a rotating cage, positional gravitational errors average out as the watch sits upright in a pocket.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tourbillon movements are among the most intricate, prized mechanical complications in luxury horology.

name: Jeweler
visual_anchor: A bench jeweler using a micro-torch and jewelers loupe to solder an intricate platinum prong setting around a brilliant-cut diamond solitaire ring.
core_traits: Designs, fabricates, repairs, and appraises fine jewelry made from precious metals and gemstones
Sets diamonds and precious stones using prong, bezel, channel, and pave micro-setting techniques
Operates jewelers saws, rolling mills, polishing wheels, laser welders, and micro-torches
Identifies gemstones using refractometers, polariscopes, gemological microscopes, and diamond testers

facts_and_myths.claim: Pure 24-karat gold is widely used for durable everyday diamond engagement rings because of its high purity.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pure 24k gold is extremely soft and bends easily under finger pressure, causing gemstones to fall out; jewelers alloy it with copper and silver (14k or 18k) for strength.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: 18-karat gold consists of 75% pure gold and 25% strengthening alloy metals.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rubies and sapphires are chemically the exact same mineral crystal called corundum.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Both are crystalline aluminum oxide (Al2O3); trace chromium creates red rubies, while iron and titanium create blue sapphires.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Any gem-quality corundum that is not red is classified by jewelers as a sapphire, including pink, yellow, and green varieties.

name: Potter
visual_anchor: A potter with clay-covered hands centering a spinning mound of wet terracotta clay on an electric potter's wheel inside a sunlit studio lined with drying ceramic vessels.
core_traits: Shapes wet clay into functional pottery and ceramic vessels using a spinning wheel or hand-building techniques
Masters clay preparation: wedging, throwing, trimming, and pulling handles
Formulates and applies mineral glazes containing silica, fluxes, and metal colorants
Fires ceramic pieces through bisque and glaze cycles in high-temperature kilns reaching up to 2,300 degrees F

facts_and_myths.claim: Ceramics and pottery represent one of the oldest synthetic human technologies in archaeological history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fired clay Venus figurines and ceramic cooking pots have been dated to over 20,000 to 29,000 years ago during the Upper Paleolithic era.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Clay undergoes an irreversible chemical change during firing called sintering, permanently transforming from soft soil into rock-hard ceramic.

facts_and_myths.claim: Pottery glaze colors look identical on wet unfired clay as they do after coming out of a 2,000-degree kiln.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unfired glazes often look like dull gray or chalky pastel liquids; intense kiln heat causes complex chemical fusion that develops brilliant glossy colors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A raw glaze containing black cobalt oxide burns into an iconic radiant deep sapphire blue.

name: Tailor
visual_anchor: A bespoke tailor with a yellow cloth measuring tape draped over their neck chalking cutting patterns onto fine British wool cloth on a large wooden cutting table.
core_traits: Designs, cuts, fits, and sews custom bespoke suits, coats, trousers, and tailored garments
Takes precise anatomical measurements of shoulder slope, chest curvature, and posture
Constructs floating canvas interlinings, hand-padded lapels, and hand-sewn buttonholes
Uses tailor's shears, tailor's chalk, steam press irons, and heavy industrial sewing machines

facts_and_myths.claim: The world-famous center of traditional bespoke men's tailoring is Savile Row in Mayfair, London.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Savile Row has hosted world-class bespoke tailoring houses like Henry Poole and Gieves & Hawkes crafting handmade suits since the 18th century.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A genuine bespoke Savile Row suit requires over 50 hours of hand craftsmanship and multiple customer fittings.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bespoke suits and off-the-rack made-to-measure suits are manufactured using identical mass-production methods.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Off-the-rack garments modify a standard digital template; genuine bespoke drafting creates an entirely unique paper pattern drafted from scratch for that client's exact physique.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word 'bespoke' comes from the historic practice of a tailor declaring a specific bolt of cloth 'bespoken' for an individual client.

name: Cobbler
visual_anchor: A traditional cobbler in a leather apron hammering wooden pegs into a replacement leather sole mounted on a cast-iron shoe lasting anvil surrounded by vintage leather boots.
core_traits: Crafts, restores, resoles, and repairs leather boots, dress shoes, and orthopedic footwear
Uses shoe lasts (foot molds), curved awls, leather skiving knives, and heavy-duty Goodyear welting machines
Replaces worn leather and rubber outsoles, rebuilds stacked leather heels, and stretches tight shoes
Stitches leather uppers, edge-dresses outsoles, and polishes footwear with carnauba wax and creams

facts_and_myths.claim: Historically, a 'cordwainer' made brand new shoes from luxury leather, while a 'cobbler' only repaired old worn shoes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In medieval English guilds, cordwainers had legal exclusivity to craft new shoes from Cordovan leather, while cobblers were legally restricted to repairs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Today the word 'cobbler' is colloquially used for both shoe repairers and bespoke shoemakers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Left and right shoes with distinct anatomical shapes have been standard throughout all of human footwear history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: For centuries, shoes were made 'straight' - identical for both feet - and wore into the shape of the foot over painful weeks of walking.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Right-and-left foot specific shoe lasts only became standard manufacturing practice in the mid-19th century.

name: Lumberjack
visual_anchor: A rugged lumberjack in a plaid flannel shirt, suspenders, and hard hat making a precise directional undercut wedge in a giant Douglas fir tree with a powerful professional chainsaw.
core_traits: Harvests timber trees in commercial forests using powerful chainsaws and heavy mechanized logging equipment
Calculates directional felling notches, hinge wood thickness, tree lean, and wind factors
Wears specialized personal protection: chainsaw chaps with Kevlar fibers, steel-toe boots, and face screens
Operates skidder tractors, feller bunchers, and log loaders to transport felled timber

facts_and_myths.claim: Protective chainsaw safety chaps are woven with long Kevlar fibers that instantly choke and stall spinning chainsaw blades.
facts_and_myths.explanation: If a spinning chain touches the fabric, thousands of high-tensile fibers pull out and wrap around the drive sprocket, jamming it in a millisecond.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chainsaw chaps have saved countless loggers from life-threatening femoral artery injuries.

facts_and_myths.claim: Lumberjacks cut down massive trees by hacking randomly at the trunk from all sides until it topples over.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Felling is a precise physics discipline involving a directional face notch, a level back cut, and a carefully preserved wood 'hinge' that steers the fall.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An experienced timber faller can place a 100-foot tree onto a stake driven into the ground with pinpoint accuracy.

name: Locomotive Engineer
visual_anchor: A locomotive engineer seated at the throttle and dynamic brake console of a heavy freight diesel locomotive looking down parallel railroad tracks winding through a river valley.
core_traits: Operates multi-thousand-ton freight and passenger diesel-electric or electric trains over railroad networks
Controls master throttle notches, automatic air brakes, and dynamic regenerative braking
Monitors wayside colored block signals, track speeds, and positive train control (PTC) computer systems
Manages train slack action and momentum across steep mountain grades and sharp track curves

facts_and_myths.claim: A mile-long fully loaded freight train traveling at 55 mph can require a full mile of distance to come to a complete stop.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Due to steel wheels on steel rails having minimal friction and immense train weight exceeding 15,000 tons, emergency stops take enormous distances.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A train cannot swerve, so the engineer's only defense when an obstruction appears on tracks is emergency air braking.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern diesel locomotives use giant diesel engines to turn the train wheels directly through a mechanical clutch.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Locomotives are diesel-electric hybrids; the massive diesel engine turns an electrical generator, which powers electric traction motors on the wheel axles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Electric traction motors provide maximum torque instantly from a dead standstill.

name: Long-Haul Truck Driver
visual_anchor: A long-haul truck driver leaning against the gleaming chrome bumper of a 18-wheel semi-truck cab at a neon-lit highway truck stop at twilight.
core_traits: Drives heavy semi-trailer commercial trucks over interstates transporting freight, food, and goods across nations
Holds a Commercial Driver's License (CDL) with air brake and hazardous cargo endorsements
Inspects truck brakes, fifth-wheel kingpin couplings, tire pressures, and electronic logging devices (ELD)
Navigates tight urban delivery docks, mountain grades with runaway truck ramps, and blizzard road conditions

facts_and_myths.claim: Over 70% of all freight tonnage moved across the United States is transported by commercial truck drivers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Trucking represents the vital backbone of supply chains; almost every grocery item, medicine, and retail good travels on a truck at some stage.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Without commercial trucking, grocery stores would face severe food shortages within 48 to 72 hours.

facts_and_myths.claim: Commercial truck drivers can legally drive continuously for 24 hours straight without taking rest breaks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Federal Hours of Service regulations mandate that drivers cannot exceed 11 hours of driving within a 14-hour duty window, verified by electronic logs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Drivers must take a mandatory 10 consecutive hours off-duty before starting a new driving cycle.

name: Bus Driver
visual_anchor: A professional municipal transit bus driver in a uniform shirt seated behind the large steering wheel of a modern city hybrid transit bus opening passenger doors at a busy station.
core_traits: Transports public passengers safely along scheduled urban municipal transit routes or cross-country coach lines
Manages automated fare collection boxes, wheelchair accessibility ramps, and passenger priority seating
Navigates large 40-foot and articulated 60-foot passenger buses through dense city traffic and tight street turns
Trained in passenger de-escalation, transit emergency protocols, and pedestrian blind-spot avoidance

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern municipal low-floor transit buses use pneumatic suspension systems to physically 'kneel' down toward street curbs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Drivers activate kneeling pneumatic valves that lower the right side entrance by several inches to allow easy boarding for elderly and mobility-impaired riders.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The kneeling bus concept was introduced in the late 1970s and revolutionized urban public transit accessibility.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bus drivers are completely unmonitored once they leave the depot and can deviate along whatever streets they prefer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Transit buses are tracked continuously by GPS dispatch centers monitoring schedule adherence, route conformance, and passenger loads in real time.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dispatchers can send real-time route detours and schedule holding instructions directly to the driver's cab console.

name: Coal Miner
visual_anchor: An underground miner with coal dust on their face wearing a heavy yellow hard hat with a bright cap lamp kneeling in a low subterranean coal seam beside a continuous mining machine.
core_traits: Extracts coal and minerals from underground mine workings hundreds or thousands of feet beneath the surface
Operates continuous miners, longwall shearers, shuttle cars, and roof bolting hydraulic drilling rigs
Monitors atmospheric explosive methane gas concentrations and oxygen levels using multi-gas detectors
Installs steel wire mesh and resin anchor bolts into stone mine roofs to prevent rock falls

facts_and_myths.claim: Coal miners historically carried live canaries in small cages into underground mine tunnels to detect toxic carbon monoxide gas.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Canaries have higher metabolic rates and sensitivity to toxic gases than humans; if the bird showed distress, miners evacuated immediately.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: British coal mines continued using canaries until digital electronic multi-gas detectors replaced them in 1986.

facts_and_myths.claim: Underground coal mines are lit by open burning candle lanterns and kerosene torches.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Open flames are strictly illegal in coal mines because invisible methane gas and coal dust can explode violently; miners use sealed, intrinsically safe cap lamps.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sir Humphry Davy invented the Davy safety lamp in 1815, which used fine wire gauze to prevent flames from igniting surrounding methane.

name: Wind Turbine Technician
visual_anchor: A wind turbine technician secured by fall-arrest lanyards standing atop the nacelle of a massive 300-foot wind turbine against a dramatic blue sky overlooking a vast prairie wind farm.
core_traits: Climbs hundreds of feet up turbine towers to inspect, service, and repair mechanical and electrical generation components
Services multi-megawatt electrical generators, yaw gearboxes, hydraulic pitch controls, and braking systems
Conducts rope-access composite blade repairs and aerodynamic leading-edge erosion fixes
Works in high-altitude confined spaces subjected to strong prairie and offshore wind gusts

facts_and_myths.claim: The tips of modern commercial wind turbine blades can slice through the air at speeds exceeding 180 miles per hour.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Even when the rotor appears to turn slowly at 12 to 20 RPM, the sheer length of 200-foot blades creates massive tip speeds near 200 mph.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Turbine blade tips move fast enough that raindrops can cause abrasive aerodynamic erosion over years of rotation.

facts_and_myths.claim: Wind turbine technicians take passenger elevators to the top of every single wind turbine tower.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most utility-scale turbine towers only feature vertical internal ladders; technicians climb 300 vertical rungs with heavy climbing harnesses daily.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Climbing a 300-foot turbine ladder is equivalent to climbing a 30-story skyscraper on foot before starting work.

name: Baker
visual_anchor: An artisan baker in a flour-dusted apron sliding a batch of golden crusty sourdough boules out of a stone hearth deck oven using a long wooden peel.
core_traits: Mixes, shapes, proofs, and bakes breads, rolls, bagels, and rustic yeast-leavened doughs
Controls fermentation biochemistry using wild sourdough yeast starters and levains
Operates high-capacity spiral dough mixers, proofing cabinets, and steam-injected stone hearth deck ovens
Scores decorative patterns on dough loaves with a razor-sharp baker's blade (lame) before baking

facts_and_myths.claim: Commercial steam injection inside deck ovens creates the crispy, glossy crust on artisan sourdough bread.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Steam condenses onto the cool dough surface, gelatinizing starches into a thin sugar glaze that hardens into a crackling golden blistered crust.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Steam also delays outer crust formation, allowing the bread to expand fully in an effect called 'oven spring'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bread dough that is kneaded continuously for hours becomes increasingly tender and softer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Over-kneading breaks down gluten protein bonds and oxidizes flour pigments, resulting in a dense, crumbly, bleached loaf.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many artisan breads use 'no-knead' or gentle coil fold techniques that rely on long natural fermentation to develop gluten structure.

name: Pastry Chef
visual_anchor: A pastry chef in a clean white coat carefully piping delicate swirls of Italian meringue onto an artistic fruit tart using a fluted pastry nozzle.
core_traits: Specializes in the delicate creation of gourmet desserts, viennoiserie, laminated croissants, and confections
Masters precise sugar chemistry, chocolate tempering, custard emulsification, and gelatin gelling points
Bakes laminated puff pastry doughs, choux pastries, macarons, and multi-tiered decorative cakes
Collaborates with restaurant kitchen brigades to design multi-course dessert tasting menus

facts_and_myths.claim: A traditional French butter croissant dough is folded repeatedly to create dozens of microscopic layers of butter and dough.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Through a meticulous folding process called lamination, a croissant typically contains 27 to 81 individual alternating layers of dough and butter.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When baked, water in the butter turns to steam, puffing up the dough layers into a flaky, honeycomb interior.

facts_and_myths.claim: Pastry recipes can be loosely eyeballed by intuition without using measuring scales or timers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Baking and pastry arts are exact food chemistry; altering sugar ratios by a few grams disrupts protein coagulation, moisture, and caramelization.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Professional pastry kitchens weigh all liquid and dry ingredients in exact grams rather than volume cups.

name: Chocolatier
visual_anchor: A chocolatier working with a flat offset spatula spreading molten glossy tempered chocolate across a cool white marble tempering slab.
core_traits: Creates luxury chocolate confections, truffles, molded pralines, and artistic edible chocolate sculptures
Masters the delicate physics of tempering cocoa butter into stable Form V beta crystals for snap and gloss
Operates continuous tempering machines, guitar cutters, enrobers, and polycarbonate chocolate molds
Pairs flavor profiles using single-origin cacao beans, fruit ganaches, nuts, and exotic spices

facts_and_myths.claim: White 'bloom' film on old chocolate means the chocolate has grown dangerous fuzzy mold and must be thrown out.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Chocolate bloom is merely cocoa butter fats or sugar crystals migrating to the surface after temperature fluctuations; it is completely harmless to eat.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bloomed chocolate can be re-tempered and melted down to look brand new and glossy again.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cocoa butter can crystallize into six different polymorphic crystalline forms, but only one form produces ideal chocolate.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Form V (Beta) crystals melt at exactly human body temperature (93-97 degrees F) and give chocolate its glossy sheen and crisp snap.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Improperly tempered chocolate melts into a soft, dull, greasy mass with no snap.

name: Sommelier
visual_anchor: A distinguished sommelier in a tailored tuxedo wearing a silver tastevin medallion gently decanting a vintage red wine by candlelight in a fine dining wine cellar.
core_traits: Trained wine professional specializing in wine service, cellar management, and food-and-wine pairings
Identifies grape varietals, vintage years, and terroir regions through blind sensory organoleptic tasting
Performs formal tableside decanting, cork inspection, and champagne sabering service
Curates international wine lists, manages cellar humidity, and evaluates craft beers, spirits, and coffees

facts_and_myths.claim: Smelling the extracted cork at a restaurant table tells you if the wine tastes delicious.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Smelling the cork merely smells like wet wood; sommeliers inspect the cork visually for mold or drying cracks, but taste the wine directly to test for spoilage.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The primary cork fault is TCA (trichloroanisole), which makes wine smell like wet cardboard or a damp basement.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Master Sommelier diploma exam has one of the lowest pass rates of any professional exam in the world.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Since its founding in 1969, fewer than 300 candidates worldwide have successfully passed the grueling Master Sommelier exam.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The blind tasting component requires candidates to identify the grape, region, and exact vintage year of six mystery wines in 25 minutes.

name: Bartender
visual_anchor: A mixologist bartender in a vintage leather apron shaking a stainless steel Boston cocktail shaker, rimming glasses with citrus peel behind a backlit craft spirits bar.
core_traits: Crafts alcoholic cocktails, mocktails, and beverages in bars, lounges, and hospitality venues
Proficient in mixology techniques: shaking, stirring, muddling, straining, and flaming garnishes
Memorizes hundreds of classic cocktail recipes like the Old Fashioned, Martini, Negroni, and Margarita
Monitors patron intoxication levels responsibly, checks age identification, and manages bar inventory

facts_and_myths.claim: James Bond's famous preference for a Martini 'shaken, not stirred' is recommended by professional bartenders for clarity.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Shaking aerates spirit-forward cocktails with tiny ice micro-chips, clouding the liquid; bartenders stir spirits-only drinks with ice to keep them crystal-clear and silky.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Shaking is strictly reserved for drinks containing citrus juice, egg whites, cream, or syrups.

facts_and_myths.claim: Tonic water glows bright fluorescent cyan under ultraviolet blacklight because it contains natural quinine.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Quinine, extracted from the bark of the South American cinchona tree, absorbs UV light and re-emits it as visible blue light.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: British colonial officers in India originally mixed bitter antimalarial quinine tonic with gin to make it palatable, inventing the Gin & Tonic.

name: Barista
visual_anchor: A barista in a denim apron pouring microfoam steamed milk into an espresso cup to create an intricate tulip latte art pattern beside a gleaming commercial espresso machine.
core_traits: Prepares, brews, and serves espresso and specialty coffee beverages in specialty cafes and coffeehouses
Calibrates coffee burr grinders by adjusting grind size micron particles to achieve balanced extraction time
Steams whole and plant-based milks into silky microfoam to craft free-pour latte art
Masters manual filter brewing methods: V60 pour-over, Chemex, Aeropress, and siphon vacuum brewers

facts_and_myths.claim: Dark roast coffee beans contain significantly more caffeine per bean than light roast coffee beans.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dark roasting burns off moisture and slight caffeine mass; light roast beans retain slightly more caffeine density per bean.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dark roasts taste stronger and more bitter due to pyrolysis caramelization, which people mistakenly correlate with higher caffeine.

facts_and_myths.claim: A single espresso shot is extracted under 9 bars of hydraulic water pressure at roughly 200 degrees Fahrenheit.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Nine bars is nine times Earth's atmospheric pressure (roughly 130 PSI), which forces water through packed coffee grounds in 25 to 30 seconds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This intense pressure emulsifies insoluble coffee oils into the golden-brown foam layer on top called 'crema'.

name: Butcher
visual_anchor: A traditional butcher wearing a striped apron and chainmail cut-resistant glove breaking down a beef side using a boning knife on a heavy end-grain maple butcher block.
core_traits: Selects, cuts, trims, bones, and prepares primal cuts of meat, poultry, and game for culinary preparation
Uses boning knives, meat cleavers, meat bandsaws, scabbards, and manual sausage stuffers
Wears protective chainmail safety gloves and cut-resistant stainless steel mesh aprons
Understands muscle anatomy, dry-aging techniques, curing brines, and whole-animal seam butchery

facts_and_myths.claim: The red liquid pooling inside raw beef steak packages in grocery stores is pure animal blood.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Nearly all blood is drained during slaughter; the red liquid is myoglobin, an oxygen-carrying muscle protein mixed with natural water.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Myoglobin turns brown when cooked or exposed to oxygen, signaling meat doneness.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dry-aging beef for 30 to 60 days in temperature-controlled humidity lockers dramatically intensifies tenderness and umami flavor.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Natural enzymes break down tough collagen connective tissues, while controlled moisture evaporation concentrates rich beef flavors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A harmless crust of white mold forms on the exterior of dry-aging beef, which is trimmed away before cutting steaks.

name: Cheesemaker
visual_anchor: A traditional cheesemaker in rubber boots and a white apron stirring golden curds with a curd harp inside a massive copper cheese vat in an Alpine dairy.
core_traits: Transforms raw or pasteurized milk into diverse varieties of aged, fresh, washed-rind, and blue cheeses
Monitors acidification cultures, curd coagulation, rennet enzyme reactions, and whey separation
Molds, presses, brines, and ages cheese wheels in humidity-controlled maturation caves (affineur)
Controls beneficial mold cultures like Penicillium roqueforti and Penicillium camemberti

facts_and_myths.claim: Mice naturally love eating aged yellow cheddar cheese more than any other food on Earth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mice are granivores whose sensitive noses are repelled by the pungent smell of aged cheese; they strongly prefer sweet grains, seeds, and peanut butter.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The cartoon image of mice hunting cheese is a medieval myth originating from cheese being left out on open shelves while grain was securely sealed in barrels.

facts_and_myths.claim: It takes approximately 10 pounds (over one gallon) of fresh milk to produce just one single pound of hard cheese.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Milk consists of roughly 87% water; when rennet curdles casein protein and butterfat, the remaining liquid whey is drained away.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Whey protein powder, popular in fitness supplements, was historically considered a waste byproduct of cheesemaking.

name: Brewmaster
visual_anchor: A brewmaster inspecting a glass hydrometer cylinder checking wort gravity beside gleaming stainless steel mash tuns and fermentation tanks in a craft brewery.
core_traits: Directs the formulation, mashing, boiling, fermentation, and packaging of craft beers and ales
Masters malted barley grain bills, hop alpha-acid isomerizations, water mineral chemistry, and yeast strains
Operates mash tuns, lauter tuns, brew kettles, heat exchangers, and conical fermenters
Controls sanitization protocols, dissolved oxygen limits, and carbonation volumes

facts_and_myths.claim: The German Beer Purity Law (Reinheitsgebot) of 1516 originally allowed only three ingredients: water, barley, and hops.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Yeast was not mentioned in the 1516 law because microorganisms were unknown; brewers relied on wild ambient fermentation until Louis Pasteur discovered yeast cells.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Reinheitsgebot is considered one of the oldest consumer food safety regulations still referenced in the world.

facts_and_myths.claim: Green and clear glass beer bottles protect beer from sunlight just as effectively as dark brown glass bottles.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Visible and UV blue light penetrates green and clear glass, reacting with hop isohumulones to produce 3-methyl-2-butene-1-thiol, causing 'skunky' beer flavor.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dark amber-brown glass blocks almost all photochemically reactive light wavelengths, protecting the beer.

name: Sushi Master
visual_anchor: An itamae sushi master in a traditional white chef coat and headband carefully slicing a pristine slab of bluefin tuna with a long, razor-sharp yanagiba knife behind a cypress counter.
core_traits: Master Japanese culinary chef specializing in the preparation of nigiri sushi, sashimi, and maki rolls
Masters the cooking, seasoning, and temperature control of seasoned sushi rice (shari)
Uses traditional Japanese single-bevel kitchen knives: yanagiba, deba, and usuba
Understands fish aging, salt-curing, vinegar-marinating (shime), and knife grain angles

facts_and_myths.claim: Traditional sushi apprentice training requires years of mastering rice preparation before ever touching raw fish.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Traditional apprentices in Japan spent up to three to five years cleaning, cooking, and fanning seasoned shari rice before training in fish cutting.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word 'sushi' historically refers to the vinegared sour rice, not the raw fish itself.

facts_and_myths.claim: Real authentic wasabi paste served in most Western sushi restaurants is 100% freshly grated Wasabia japonica root.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Real wasabi root is extremely rare and expensive; over 95% of restaurant wasabi is common European horseradish tinted green with food coloring.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Real freshly grated wasabi root loses its delicate pungency within 15 minutes of being grated on sharkskin.

name: Farmer
visual_anchor: A hardworking farmer in denim overalls and a wide-brimmed straw hat standing in a golden wheat field at sunrise beside a modern green combine harvester.
core_traits: Cultivates crops and raises agricultural produce to provide food, feed, and fiber for humanity
Operates heavy agricultural machinery including tractors, seed drills, and combine harvesters
Manages soil nutrients, crop rotation, irrigation schedules, and integrated pest management
Monitors weather patterns, commodity market prices, and seasonal harvest yields

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern commercial farmers rely on satellite GPS and automated steering to plant crops in dead-straight rows.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Precision agriculture uses RTK GPS receivers on tractors that steer automatically within one inch of accuracy across vast fields.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Farmers use infrared drone imagery to spot nitrogen deficiencies in individual plant rows before symptoms are visible to human eyes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Over 90% of global farms are owned by faceless multinational corporate conglomerates.
facts_and_myths.explanation: According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), roughly 90% of the world's 570 million farms are family-operated farms.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Family farms produce roughly 80% of the world's total food supply by value.

name: Beekeeper
visual_anchor: A beekeeper in a white protective bee suit and veiled hood holding a wooden honeycomb frame covered in buzzing honeybees with a smoking hive smoker nearby.
core_traits: Maintains colonies of honeybees in modern Langstroth beehives to produce honey, beeswax, and royal jelly
Wears a protective white ventilated bee suit, veil, and goatskin beekeeping gloves
Calms bees using a bee smoker fueled by wood shavings or dried pine needles
Provides vital commercial agricultural pollination services for almond, apple, and berry orchards

facts_and_myths.claim: Pure natural honey stored in sealed containers never spoils or rots over thousands of years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Honey has low moisture content (under 18%) and high acidity (pH ~3.9), creating an osmotic environment where bacteria cannot survive.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Archaeologists excavating 3,000-year-old Egyptian pharaoh tombs discovered still-edible, preserved pots of raw honey.

facts_and_myths.claim: The smoke used by beekeepers acts as a toxic sedative gas that puts guard bees to sleep.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Smoke masks the bees' alarm pheromones (isopentyl acetate) and triggers an ancient survival instinct to gorge on honey in case of forest fire, making them docile.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Full-bellied bees are physically less capable of bending their abdomens to deliver a sting.

name: Rancher
visual_anchor: A weathered rancher in a felt cowboy hat, leather chaps, and boots riding a quarter horse across an open western pasture driving a herd of Black Angus cattle.
core_traits: Breeds, grazes, and manages large herds of beef cattle, horses, or sheep on expansive open rangelands
Skilled in horsemanship, lariat rope roping, fence maintenance, and cattle branding/tagging
Monitors pasture forage rotation, drought water tanks, and veterinary herd vaccinations
Maintains remote ranch infrastructure, windmills, and all-terrain ranch vehicles

facts_and_myths.claim: Traditional cowboy ten-gallon hats were named because they could hold ten gallons of drinking water inside the crown.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The name comes from the Spanish word 'galon', referring to narrow braided ribbon bands decorating the hat brim; a real hat holds less than a gallon.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: John B. Stetson invented the 'Boss of the Plains' felt hat in 1865 to provide waterproof sun and rain protection.

facts_and_myths.claim: Livestock brand markings on cattle have been legally registered as official property deeds in the American West for over a century.
facts_and_myths.explanation: State livestock brand registries protect against cattle rustling, and registered hot-iron or freeze brands are recognized legal proof of ownership.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Freeze branding uses liquid nitrogen chilled copper irons that destroy dark pigment cells, causing white hair to grow in the brand pattern.

name: Shepherd
visual_anchor: A lone shepherd holding a traditional wooden crook standing on a misty highland hillside with a loyal border collie herding a white flock of sheep.
core_traits: Tends, pastures, and guards flocks of sheep or goats across remote hillsides and mountain meadows
Uses a shepherd's crook to catch animals by the hock and guide wandering lambs
Directs trained working herding dogs using ultrasonic whistles and spoken directional commands
Supervises spring lambing, seasonal pasture migration (transhumance), and annual fleece shearing

facts_and_myths.claim: Sheep have panoramic visual fields exceeding 300 degrees without needing to turn their heads.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Horizontal rectangular pupils allow grazing sheep to scan the horizon continuously for approaching predators while keeping their heads down.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The only blind spot for a grazing sheep is directly behind its tail.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sheep will voluntarily shed their heavy wool fleece naturally every spring without needing human shearing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Domestic sheep breeds like Merinos were selectively bred over millennia to produce continuous wool growth; without shearing, overgrown wool causes heatstroke and blindness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A famous escaped sheep in New Zealand named Shrek evaded shearing for six years and grew 60 pounds of wool.

name: Commercial Fisherman
visual_anchor: A commercial fisherman in bright yellow oilskin waterproof bibs hauling a heavy steel king crab pot out of icy Bering Sea waters on a rolling vessel deck.
core_traits: Harvests wild ocean fish, crabs, and seafood using trawling nets, longlines, and heavy pot traps
