Works in perilous offshore conditions featuring freezing spray, stormy sea states, and heavy hydraulic machinery
Wears heavy-duty PVC oilskins, steel-toe rubber boots, and neoprene deck gloves
Guts, sorts, ices, and preserves seafood catches in sub-zero refrigerated fish holds

facts_and_myths.claim: Commercial offshore crab fishing in the Bering Sea consistently ranks among the most statistically dangerous jobs on Earth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bitter sub-zero Arctic winds, heavy swinging 800-pound steel pots, and icy rolling decks cause high occupational fatality rates from man-overboard accidents.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Crews routinely work 20-hour shifts in freezing spray to prevent vessel capsizing from ice accumulation on upper decks.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern commercial trawler captains locate fish schools purely by watching seagulls dive from the deck.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern vessels utilize multi-beam hydroacoustic sonars, satellite ocean temperature maps, and acoustic net sounders to pinpoint schools miles away.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Net-monitoring sensors tell the captain the exact tonnage of fish swimming into the trawl opening in real time.

name: Park Ranger
visual_anchor: A dedicated park ranger in a tan uniform and wide-brimmed flat-hat standing at the rim of the Grand Canyon surveying visitor trails with binoculars.
core_traits: Protects national and state park natural ecosystems, wildlife habitats, and historic cultural monuments
Wears the iconic wide-brimmed campaign flat-hat, badge, and ranger duty uniform
Conducts backcountry search-and-rescue, wilderness trail patrols, and park visitor education
Enforces wildlife conservation laws and investigates illegal poaching and timber harvesting

facts_and_myths.claim: Feeding wild bears in national parks is harmless and helps them survive harsh winter months.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Human food habituates bears to human campgrounds, leading to aggressive encounters that require rangers to euthanize the animal ('A fed bear is a dead bear').
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Park rangers enforce bear-proof metal food lockers and canisters throughout wilderness backcountry zones.

facts_and_myths.claim: Yellowstone was established in 1872 as the world's very first designated national park.
facts_and_myths.explanation: President Ulysses S. Grant signed the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act dedicated to preserving geothermal wonders for future generations.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Before civilian park rangers were organized, the U.S. Army Cavalry patrolled and guarded Yellowstone from poachers.

name: Forest Ranger
visual_anchor: A forest ranger standing in a high-elevation fire lookout tower scanning a vast horizon of pine forests with an Osborne Fire Finder spotting circle.
core_traits: Manages state and national forest lands for sustainable timber, watershed health, and wildfire prevention
Operates forest fire lookout towers, weather monitoring stations, and prescribed burn operations
Measures tree stand density, basal area, timber volume, and invasive pest tree infestations using Biltmore sticks
Coordinates wildland fire suppression and watershed erosion control projects

facts_and_myths.claim: Every single wild forest fire is an unnatural catastrophe that must be extinguished within minutes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Many forest ecosystems, such as giant sequoia and ponderosa pine forests, naturally require periodic low-intensity fires to clear brush and open seed cones.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Decades of total fire suppression caused hazardous fuel build-ups that modern foresters manage with controlled prescribed burns.

facts_and_myths.claim: The famous fire lookout tool 'Osborne Fire Finder' uses topographic maps and directional sights to pinpoint forest fire coordinates.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Invented in 1911 by William Osborne, the rotating circular alidade table allows lookout rangers to report precise azimuth angles to dispatchers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: By crossing azimuth lines from two different fire towers, dispatchers triangulate the exact map coordinate of smoke within seconds.

name: Safari Guide
visual_anchor: A safari guide in khaki field bushwear holding a spotting scope seated on the raised tracker seat of an open-top 4x4 vehicle watching a pride of lions on the Serengeti.
core_traits: Leads wildlife game drives and walking safaris through wilderness reserves in Africa and Asia
Interprets animal footprint tracks, alarm calls, scat, and behavioral cues to track elusive big game
Trained in rifle ballistics, dangerous animal charge deterrence, and wilderness survival
Educates guests on conservation biology, ornithology, botany, and anti-poaching initiatives

facts_and_myths.claim: Safari guides look for bird alarm calls and oxpecker birds to locate hidden resting predators.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Prey animals and birds emit distinct sharp alarm vocalizations when a leopard or lion prowls nearby, alerting seasoned guides.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Guineafowl and baboons make unmistakable racket that guides use as natural radar to find resting big cats.

facts_and_myths.claim: Running away at top sprinting speed is the safest reaction if charged by a wild lion or elephant on foot.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Running immediately triggers a predator's predatory chase instinct; guides are trained to stand perfectly still, hold ground, and look large.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many animal charges are 'mock charges' intended to test whether the intruder will panic and flee.

name: Mountain Guide
visual_anchor: An IFMGA-certified mountain guide in glacier sunglasses and climbing harness short-roping a client across a snowy knife-edge alpine ridge in the French Alps.
core_traits: Leads clients on technical rock, ice, glacier, and high-altitude mountaineering ascents
Holds rigorous IFMGA/UIAGM mountain guide certification across ski mountaineering, rock, and alpine disciplines
Assesses snowpack avalanche risks, weather storm fronts, and glacier crevasse hazards
Masters short-roping techniques, ice screw anchor placement, and high-altitude crevasse rescue systems

facts_and_myths.claim: Mountaineers climb Mount Everest in single-day continuous sprints from base camp without stopping to acclimatize.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sudden exposure to Everest's 'Death Zone' above 8,000 meters causes fatal cerebral or pulmonary edema; climbers take weeks moving up and down camps to acclimatize.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Acclimatization stimulates bone marrow to produce millions of extra red blood cells to transport scarce oxygen.

facts_and_myths.claim: The elite mountain guide certification (IFMGA carnet) takes over 5 to 10 years of grueling examinations to attain.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Guides must pass brutal international exams in steep rock climbing, multi-day ski touring, ice climbing, and avalanche assessment.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fewer than 6,000 mountain guides in the entire world hold the full international IFMGA carnet pin.

name: Dog Groomer
visual_anchor: A pet groomer wearing a waterproof apron using curved grooming shears to fluff and scissor the curly coat of a standard poodle on an electric hydraulic grooming table.
core_traits: Bathes, clips, styles, and grooms domestic dogs and pets for hygiene, comfort, and breed standards
Operates high-velocity pet dryers, hydraulic grooming tables, and professional electric clippers
Trims canine nails with safety clippers, cleans ear canals, and expresses anal glands
Understands distinct AKC breed styling cuts, hand-stripping of terrier coats, and canine behavioral calming

facts_and_myths.claim: The traditional continental poodle haircut with pom-poms was invented purely as a frivolous luxury fashion statement.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Poodles were originally water retrievers; the cut shaved heavy wet hair for swimming speed while leaving warm woolly fur over vital joints and organs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The pom-pom on the poodle's tail was tied with a bright ribbon so hunters could spot the dog swimming in tall reeds.

facts_and_myths.claim: Shaving double-coated dogs like Huskies and Golden Retrievers in summer actually makes them hotter and damages their coat.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The dense undercoat traps air that insulates against both heat and cold, while the top guard hairs protect against sunburn.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Shaving a double coat can ruin hair follicles permanently, leading to patchy alopecia.

name: Animal Trainer
visual_anchor: An animal trainer using a target stick and clicker to guide an obedient golden retriever service dog through an obstacle course inside a specialized training arena.
core_traits: Trains domestic animals, marine mammals, or exotic wildlife for assistance, security, or film entertainment
Applies operant conditioning principles: positive reinforcement, clicker marker cues, and shaping behaviors
Trains guide dogs for the blind, medical alert dogs for seizures, and search-and-rescue canines
Designs desensitization protocols to habituate animals to loud crowds, flash photography, and movie sets

facts_and_myths.claim: The dominant 'alpha wolf' pack theory is the scientific foundation for training obedient domestic dogs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The original 1940s 'alpha wolf' study was conducted on unrelated captive wolves in artificial stress; natural wolf packs are cooperative family units led by parents.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern animal behaviorists train via positive reward motivation rather than dominance force.

facts_and_myths.claim: Guide dogs for the visually impaired are trained to practice 'intelligent disobedience' when commanded into danger.
facts_and_myths.explanation: If a handler commands 'Forward' but an oncoming car or open manhole poses a lethal threat, the guide dog refuses to move forward.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Teaching a dog when to deliberately disobey a command is one of the most advanced milestones in guide dog training.

name: Wildlife Photographer
visual_anchor: A camouflaged wildlife photographer lying prone in a marsh blind peering through an 800mm telephoto lens mounted on a gimbal tripod tracking a leaping snow leopard.
core_traits: Captures high-resolution photographic images of wild animals, bird species, and ecosystems in their natural habitats
Operates professional DSLR/mirrorless camera bodies, massive super-telephoto prime lenses, and DSLR camera traps
Waits silently for hours or weeks inside camouflaged photographic hides in freezing cold or tropical heat
Understands animal habits, natural lighting angles, shutter speeds, and ethical non-intrusive wildlife distances

facts_and_myths.claim: Wildlife photographers use giant telephoto lenses primarily so they never have to wait in the wild.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Photographers often spend months living in sub-zero blinds or mosquito-infested swamps just to capture a single fleeting five-second behavioral moment.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Renowned photographer Vincent Munier spent weeks in minus 35-degree Tibetan blizzards tracking the ghost-like snow leopard.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern wildlife photographers deploy infrared sensor camera traps that fire automatically when an animal steps in front.
facts_and_myths.explanation: DSLR camera traps with wireless strobes enable photographers to capture intimate close-ups of shy nocturnal animals in complete darkness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Camera traps have captured the first photographic evidence of species previously thought to be extinct.

name: Film Director
visual_anchor: A visionary film director wearing headphones seated in a folding canvas director's chair staring intensely at a high-definition video village monitor on a bustling movie set.
core_traits: Controls the artistic, dramatic, and visual aspects of motion pictures, guiding actors and film crew
Translates script screenplays into cinematic shots using shot lists, storyboards, and director's viewfinders
Directs actor performances, camera framing, lighting moods, soundscapes, and set pacing
Works with editors during post-production to finalize the definitive director's cut

facts_and_myths.claim: Film directors personally operate the heavy movie camera on their shoulder throughout every scene.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The camera is operated by the camera operator under the direction of the Director of Photography (DP); the director focuses on performance and storytelling.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Directors observe scenes primarily through video monitors called 'video village'.

facts_and_myths.claim: The black-and-white clapperboard (slate) is used to synchronize recorded sound with moving image film frames.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The loud sharp clapping sound creates an instant spike on audio waveforms that matches the exact visual frame the hinged stick touches.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The slate also visually displays the scene number, take number, roll, and director's name for post-production editors.

name: Cinematographer
visual_anchor: A cinematographer with a light meter around their neck peering through the eyepiece of a heavy digital cinema camera mounted on a hydraulic studio dolly track.
core_traits: Chief of camera and lighting crews responsible for the photographic look, color palette, and visual mood of a film
Selects cinema camera systems, anamorphic and spherical prime lenses, shutter angles, and depth-of-field
Designs three-point lighting setups using key lights, fill lights, rim lights, and colored gel diffusions
Collaborates with the gaffer and key grip to execute complex camera dolly, jib crane, and Steadicam movements

facts_and_myths.claim: Cinematographers only choose camera lenses and do not manage lighting fixtures on film sets.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lighting is the single most important artistic tool of a cinematographer; they sculpt every shadow and highlight using dozens of lighting instruments.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The cinematographer directs both the camera crew and the entire lighting (electric) and grip departments.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cinematic films have traditionally been shot at a standardized frame rate of 24 frames per second since the 1920s.
facts_and_myths.explanation: 24 fps was established as the minimum speed necessary to reproduce clear optical sound tracks smoothly on early synchronized sound film.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: 24 fps gives cinema its distinctive motion blur aesthetic, distinct from high-frame-rate video.

name: Actor
visual_anchor: A dramatic thespian in period theatrical costume standing on a wooden stage delivering an impassioned monologue under a brilliant spotlight in an ornate theatre.
core_traits: Portrays dramatic characters in theater plays, motion pictures, television series, and live productions
Memorizes extensive script dialogue, stage blocking, subtext motivations, and emotional character arcs
Utilizes acting techniques: Stanislavski system, Method acting, Meisner technique, and voice projection
Collaborates with directors and fellow actors during rehearsals and multiple film takes

facts_and_myths.claim: The ancient Greek word 'Thespian' comes from Thespis, the first actor recorded to step out of a chorus to speak dialogue.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In ancient Greece around 534 BC, Thespis stepped forward from the dithyramb chorus to speak dialogue as a separate character, inventing acting.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The traditional theatrical comedy and tragedy masks are called Thalia and Melpomene.

facts_and_myths.claim: Saying 'Good luck' to an actor before walking on stage is considered an auspicious tradition.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In theatrical superstition, wishing 'good luck' invites bad luck; actors traditionally say 'Break a leg' instead to avoid tempting evil spirits.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Actors also avoid uttering the name of Shakespeare's play 'Macbeth' inside a theater, referring to it as 'The Scottish Play'.

name: Voice Actor
visual_anchor: A voice actor wearing studio monitor headphones speaking animatedly into a gold-sputtered condenser microphone fitted with a pop filter inside a padded soundproof vocal booth.
core_traits: Provides vocal performances for animated films, video game characters, audiobooks, commercials, and ADR dubbing
Masters vocal modulation, dialect accents, character voices, and emotional intensity using only the voice
Performs in acoustically treated isolation booths reading scripts on stands without rustling paper noise
Synchronizes speech precisely to existing visual mouth animation (lip-syncing and automated dialogue replacement)

facts_and_myths.claim: Voice actors record line reads while watching the finished, fully rendered animation playing on screens.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Western animation, voice actors record dialogue first; animators draw the characters' mouth movements and expressions to match the actor's vocal performance.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Only foreign language dubbing requires matching existing finished animated mouth movements.

facts_and_myths.claim: Legendary voice actor Mel Blanc voiced nearly all of the classic Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Known as 'The Man of a Thousand Voices', Blanc voiced Bugs Bunny, Porky Pig, Tweety Bird, Barney Rubble, and dozens more iconic characters.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When Blanc was in a coma following a 1961 car crash, a doctor woke him by asking 'Bugs, how are you today?' and Blanc answered in Bugs Bunny's voice.

name: Musician
visual_anchor: A virtuoso musician playing an acoustic grand piano on a concert stage, warm spotlight reflecting off polished black lacquer and fluttering sheet music.
core_traits: Performs, composes, and arranges musical pieces using vocal or instrumental instruments
Reads sheet music notation, chord charts, musical tempos, and expressive dynamic markings
Practices thousands of hours of technical scale fingerings, breath control, and tone intonation
Performs in symphony orchestras, rock bands, jazz ensembles, or solo concert recitals

facts_and_myths.claim: Listening to Mozart's classical music as an infant permanently boosts human IQ scores by twenty points.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The sensationalized 'Mozart Effect' was a misinterpretation of a 1993 study showing only a temporary 15-minute spatial reasoning boost in college students.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: However, actively learning to play a musical instrument physically enlarges the corpus callosum connecting the brain's hemispheres.

facts_and_myths.claim: The world's most prized classical violins were crafted in Cremona, Italy, in the 17th and 18th centuries by Antonio Stradivari.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Surviving 'Stradivarius' violins are acoustic masterpieces renowned for their rich tonal resonance and sell for tens of millions of dollars.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tree ring dendrochronology shows Stradivari used spruce wood that grew during Europe's 'Little Ice Age', producing unusually dense wood rings.

name: Orchestra Conductor
visual_anchor: A maestro conductor in a formal black tailcoat standing on an elevated podium sweeping a slender white fiberglass baton to direct a 100-piece symphony orchestra.
core_traits: Directs musical ensembles and symphony orchestras during rehearsals and live classical performances
Communicates tempo, time signatures, musical phrasing, and dynamic entries using a lightweight baton and hand gestures
Interprets complex multi-instrument orchestral master scores simultaneously across strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion
Balances harmonic balance, sectional entrances, and artistic emotional interpretation

facts_and_myths.claim: The orchestra conductor is merely a decorative figure waving a stick while musicians follow their own sheet music.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because sound travels slowly across a 100-person stage, musicians cannot listen to each other; they depend completely on the conductor's visual beat for synchronization.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The conductor conducts rehearsals for weeks, deciding the exact articulation, balance, and artistic soul of the performance.

facts_and_myths.claim: Early orchestral conductors used heavy wooden staffs to pound time loudly on the wooden stage floor.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the 17th century, Jean-Baptiste Lully notoriously struck his own foot with his heavy wooden conducting staff, developed gangrene, and died from the wound.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Following Lully's death, conductors transitioned to silent paper rolls and eventually the slender modern lightweight baton.

name: Opera Singer
visual_anchor: A dramatic operatic soprano in an elaborate baroque velvet gown singing a powerful aria with arms open wide on an ornate European opera house stage.
core_traits: Classical vocalist trained in unamplified vocal projection across major acoustic theater halls
Masters operatic vocal classifications: Soprano, Mezzo-Soprano, Contralto, Tenor, Baritone, and Bass
Sings complex classical librettos in Italian, German, French, and Russian without microphones
Combines bel canto vocal technique, diaphragm breath support, and theatrical character acting

facts_and_myths.claim: Professional opera singers use hidden wireless lapel microphones concealed in their costumes to project sound.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Classical opera is strictly 100% acoustic and unamplified; singers train for a decade to vibrate their pharyngeal cavities to project over an entire orchestra.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This acoustic phenomenon is called the 'singer's formant' - a resonant frequency peak around 3,000 Hz where the human ear is most sensitive.

facts_and_myths.claim: An opera singer's powerful voice can shatter a real crystal wine glass by singing the glass's resonant pitch.
facts_and_myths.explanation: If a singer sustains the exact natural resonant frequency of crystal glass with sufficient volume, acoustic resonance amplifies vibrations until the crystal fractures.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: MythBusters famously proved that rock vocalist Jaime Vendera could shatter a wine glass using purely unamplified vocal power.

name: Ballet Dancer
visual_anchor: A prima ballerina in a white tulle tutu and pink satin pointe shoes executing an exquisite arabesque balance on the tip of her toes on a theatrical stage.
core_traits: Performs classical and contemporary choreographed ballet works through athletic and artistic dance
Dances en pointe using reinforced satin pointe shoes padded with toe tape or lambswool
Executes technical ballet movements: pirouettes, grand jetes, arabesques, and fouette turns
Maintains extreme physical flexibility, core muscular strength, turnout alignment, and balance

facts_and_myths.claim: The reinforced hard toe box of a ballerina's pointe shoe is constructed of wood or metal.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pointe shoes are constructed of tightly packed layers of burlap, canvas, and cardboard glued together with specialized flour paste.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A principal ballerina can wear out and break a pair of pointe shoes in a single evening performance.

facts_and_myths.claim: During a classical 32-turn fouette sequence in Swan Lake, the ballerina's whipping leg stores rotational momentum.
facts_and_myths.explanation: By opening her working leg outward and snapping it inward, the dancer conserves angular momentum to keep spinning without losing balance.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dancers fix their gaze on a single focal point in the audience (spotting) to prevent dizziness during rapid spins.

name: Circus Acrobat
visual_anchor: A circus aerialist in a glittering sequined bodysuit executing a dramatic split suspension from dual hanging red silk fabrics high above a circus arena.
core_traits: Performs daring gymnastic aerial stunts, contortions, and feats of physical balance in circus shows
Specializes in aerial apparatus: flying trapeze, aerial silk ribbons, lyra hoops, and Chinese poles
Executes high-altitude mid-air catches, somersault releases, and hand-to-hand balancing
Trains in rigorous fall-safety mechanics, net dismounts, and apparatus rigging inspection

facts_and_myths.claim: Flying trapeze artists catch each other purely by gripping each other's fingertips in mid-air.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Aerialists use a secure interlocking wrist-to-forearm grip; fingertip grips would slip instantly under multi-G centrifugal swing forces.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Aerialists dust their hands and arms with magnesium chalk to prevent moisture slippage during catches.

facts_and_myths.claim: French acrobat Jules Leotard invented both the flying trapeze act and the skin-tight one-piece garment named after him.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1859, Leotard performed the first trapeze transfer act in Paris wearing a streamlined knitted suit that became the universal dance 'leotard'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Leotard's daring flights over padded mattresses made him a global celebrity whose name entered the English language.

name: Magician
visual_anchor: A charismatic magician in a black tuxedo jacket spreading a deck of cards in a perfect mid-air cascade while holding a silver-tipped magic wand.
core_traits: Entertains audiences through theatrical illusions, sleight of hand, mentalism, and stage escapes
Masters deception psychology, misdirection of attention, optical angles, and prop mechanics
Performs classic stage illusions: sawing a person in half, levitations, vanishing birds, and card palming
Guards the professional secrets of magic techniques bound by the Magician's Oath

facts_and_myths.claim: Sleight of hand relies primarily on moving your fingers faster than the human eye can physically see.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Human vision easily tracks fast motions; sleight of hand works through cognitive misdirection - directing the audience's attention elsewhere at the critical moment.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Magicians exploit the brain's natural tendency to assume continuity in visual motion.

facts_and_myths.claim: Harry Houdini made a career out of publicly exposing fraudulent spiritualist mediums and psychic tricksters.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Houdini used his mastery of illusion and lock mechanics to debunk fake seances and spirit photography that exploited grieving families.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Before he died, Houdini gave his wife a secret coded message to see if any real medium could contact him after death; none ever did.

name: Stunt Performer
visual_anchor: A stunt performer in flame-retardant gel and protective pads leaping backwards through a shattered breakaway sugar-glass window amidst an explosion fireball.
core_traits: Executes dangerous physical action sequences in motion pictures and television doubling for lead actors
Specializes in high falls into air bags, precision car crashes, full-body fire burns, and wirework stunts
Wears specialized protective equipment: fire retardant Zel-Jel, carbon fiber body armor, and jerk harnesses
Calculates physics trajectories, breakaway prop strengths, and pyrotechnic timing clearances

facts_and_myths.claim: Breakaway stunt glass in action movies is made of real pane glass coated with baby oil.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Real glass produces razor-sharp shards; movie stunt glass is crafted from brittle melted sugar or translucent optical polyurethane resin that crumbles safely.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sugar glass was originally made by boiling sugar, corn syrup, and water until it cooled into clear sheets.

facts_and_myths.claim: Stunt performers executing full-body fire burns wear cold fireproof carbon gels under Nomex suits.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Performers wear multiple layers of flame-retardant Nomex soaked in freezing thermal protective gel and must hold their breath to avoid inhaling searing flames.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A full-body burn stunt typically lasts no more than 20 to 30 seconds before safety crew extinguish the performer with CO2.

name: Ringmaster
visual_anchor: A theatrical ringmaster in a scarlet red tailcoat, shiny top hat, and white gloves sweeping his arm with a booming microphone inside an illuminated center circus ring.
core_traits: Master of ceremonies who introduces circus acts, directs audience attention, and paces the live production
Traditionally dressed in an iconic scarlet tailcoat with gold epaulets, top hat, and riding boots
Delivers theatrical booming vocal introductions ('Ladies and gentlemen, children of all ages!')
Maintains show timing, fills unexpected equipment delays, and cues live circus brass bands

facts_and_myths.claim: The traditional circus ring is standardized at exactly 42 feet (13 meters) in diameter across the world.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Philip Astley determined in 1768 that a 42-foot circle creates the ideal centrifugal force for acrobatic riders to stand upright on galloping horses.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The 42-foot dimension remains the standard international ring size for circuses worldwide to this day.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ringmasters traditionally carried whips to physically strike circus performers who made mistakes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The whip was used to cue equestrian horses with sound cues (the crack of the whip over their heads), never to strike human performers or animals.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The crack of a whip is actually a miniature sonic boom created when the tip breaks the speed of sound.

name: Sculptor
visual_anchor: A sculptor in an artist smock using a pointed steel chisel and wooden mallet to carve the drapery folds of a classical human torso out of a block of Carrara marble.
core_traits: Creates three-dimensional fine art forms by carving marble, casting bronze, or modeling clay and plaster
Masters subtractive techniques (stone carving) and additive techniques (clay modeling and bronze casting)
Uses pneumatic chisels, rasps, rifflers, pointing machines, and lost-wax investment molds
Understands 3D spatial proportions, human musculoskeletal anatomy, and dynamic center of gravity

facts_and_myths.claim: Ancient Greek and Roman marble classical statues were originally sculpted in pure unpainted white stone.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Ancient marble statues were painted in vivid, brilliant colors; centuries of burial and weathering washed away pigments, leaving bare white stone.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ultraviolet light analysis and chemical spectroscopy reveal bright reds, blues, and gold leaf on classical statues.

facts_and_myths.claim: Michelangelo carved his monumental 17-foot statue of David out of a flawed marble block abandoned by other sculptors.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The massive marble block from Carrara had been quarried 40 years earlier and abandoned as ruined until Michelangelo took it over in 1501.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Michelangelo famously claimed: 'Every block of stone has a statue inside it and it is the task of the sculptor to discover it.'

name: Painter
visual_anchor: A painter in a paint-splattered smock holding a wooden kidney palette mixing vibrant oil pigments with a palette knife before a large canvas mounted on a wooden easel.
core_traits: Applies artistic pigment media to canvas, wood panels, or walls to create visual fine art
Masters oil paints, acrylics, watercolors, tempera, and gouache using bristle brushes and palette knives
Understands color theory, complementary palettes, linear perspective, and chiaroscuro lighting
Prepares canvases with gesso primer, stretches linen canvases, and applies protective dammar varnish

facts_and_myths.claim: Vincent van Gogh famously cut off his entire ear and mailed it to a lover.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Historical medical records and witness accounts indicate Van Gogh severed only a portion of his left earlobe during an acute mental breakdown in Arles in 1888.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Van Gogh sold only one or two paintings during his lifetime, yet today his masterpieces sell for hundreds of millions.

facts_and_myths.claim: The historical pigment 'Ultramarine' was once more valuable than pure gold weight-for-weight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: True natural ultramarine was made by grinding semi-precious lapis lazuli gemstones mined exclusively in remote mountains of Afghanistan.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Renaissance patrons had to write separate contracts promising to supply the lapis lazuli when commissioning painters to paint the Virgin Mary's blue robe.

name: Fashion Designer
visual_anchor: A haute couture fashion designer draping flowing crimson silk fabric on a dressmaker's mannequin pinned with silver tailor pins inside a bright atelier studio.
core_traits: Creates original apparel, clothing lines, haute couture collections, and fashion accessories
Drapes fabrics directly on dressmaker mannequins, sketches fashion croquis, and selects textile materials
Directs runway fashion shows during global fashion weeks in Paris, Milan, New York, and London
Researches historical trend forecasting, silhouette trends, textile draping, and garment construction

facts_and_myths.claim: High heels were originally invented and worn by male Persian cavalry soldiers in the 10th century.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Heels locked the cavalry soldier's feet securely into riding stirrups when standing up to shoot arrows from galloping warhorses.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: King Louis XIV of France later popularized red high heels as a symbol of royal aristocratic masculinity and status.

facts_and_myths.claim: Any clothing brand can legally label their garments 'Haute Couture' on tags.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Haute Couture is a legally protected designation in France strictly granted by the Ministry of Industry to accredited Paris ateliers meeting rigorous handmade criteria.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An accredited couture house must create custom made-to-measure pieces with at least 15 full-time atelier artisans.

name: Makeup Artist
visual_anchor: A professional makeup artist using an illuminated vanity mirror and contour brushes applying precision cosmetic blending to an actor on a film production trailer.
core_traits: Applies cosmetic and prosthetic enhancements to human faces and bodies for beauty, runway, or film transformations
Applies foundations, contouring pigments, airbrush cosmetics, and corrective skin tones
Sculpts, casts, and blends foam latex and silicone prosthetic appliances for special effects (SFX) monsters and aging
Maintains strict cosmetic sanitization standards to prevent cross-contamination between clients

facts_and_myths.claim: Movie monsters and zombie makeup in modern Hollywood are created exclusively with computer-generated CGI.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Practical prosthetic makeup remains the industry gold standard for tactile realism; actors spend 3 to 6 hours daily having sculpted silicone appliances glued to their faces.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Special effects artists use alcohol-activated makeup palettes that do not smudge under hot movie studio lighting.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ancient Egyptians of all social classes wore dark kohl eyeliner to protect their eyes from desert sun glare and eye infections.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kohl was formulated from galena (lead sulfide) and copper ores, which reduced harsh sun glare and contained natural antibacterial properties.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Both Egyptian men and women lined their eyes as a matter of daily health and spiritual protection.

name: Tattoo Artist
visual_anchor: A tattoo artist wearing black nitrile gloves leaning over an arm operating a buzzing rotary tattoo machine depositing black ink lines under an articulated LED task light.
core_traits: Applies permanent decorative designs, portraits, and lettering onto human skin using specialized electric tattoo machines
Deposits sterile pigment into the dermis skin layer using sterile needle cartridges
Masters artistic drawing styles: Traditional Americana, Japanese Irezumi, Black and Grey realism, and Neo-Traditional
Enforces medical autoclave sterilization, cross-contamination prevention, and bloodborne pathogen protocols

facts_and_myths.claim: Tattoo ink is injected into the outermost surface layer of human skin cells (the epidermis).
facts_and_myths.explanation: The epidermis continuously sheds dead skin cells every month; tattoo needles deposit ink into the deeper, stable dermis layer where immune macrophages trap the pigment permanently.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If tattoo ink were injected only into the epidermis, the tattoo would disappear completely within 30 days.

facts_and_myths.claim: Otzi the Iceman, a 5,300-year-old preserved mummy found in the Alps, had 61 real tattoos on his body.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Otzi's tattoos consisted of grouped parallel lines over joints and lumbar spine, likely made by rubbing soot into cuts as therapeutic acupuncture.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Otzi provides the oldest direct physical evidence of human tattooing discovered so far.

name: Olympic Gymnast
visual_anchor: An elite gymnast with chalked hands frozen in a flawless iron cross position on the stationary wooden gymnastic rings inside an Olympic stadium.
core_traits: Competes in elite artistic gymnastic apparatus: balance beam, uneven bars, vault, floor, pommel horse, and rings
Executes high-difficulty acrobatic skills: double-layout somersaults, Tsukahara vaults, and handstand presses
Coats hands in magnesium carbonate gym chalk to absorb sweat and secure apparatus grip
Judged under the international Code of Points scoring Difficulty (D-score) and Execution (E-score)

facts_and_myths.claim: Nadia Comaneci was awarded the first 'Perfect 10' in Olympic gymnastics history in 1976, breaking the scoreboard.
facts_and_myths.explanation: At the 1976 Montreal Olympics, scoreboards were only built with three digits (max 9.99), so her perfect score was displayed as '1.00'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Comaneci went on to receive seven perfect 10s during that single Olympic competition.

facts_and_myths.claim: Olympic gymnasts can achieve gold medals relying solely on natural physical flexibility without weight training.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gymnastics demands some of the highest strength-to-weight ratios in all human sports to withstand landing forces exceeding 10 times body weight.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Male gymnasts holding an 'iron cross' on the rings exert over 300 pounds of pulling force across their shoulder ligaments.

name: Boxing Referee
visual_anchor: A boxing referee in a light blue collared shirt and black bow tie stepping between two heavyweight fighters in a square ring waving his arms to signal a fight stoppage.
core_traits: Enforces the Marquess of Queensberry rules and protects fighter safety inside professional boxing rings
Issues ring commands: 'Stop', 'Box', and 'Break' to regulate infighting and clean separations
Performs standing eight-counts, checks pupil responses, and waves off fights when a boxer cannot defend themselves
Inspects hand wraps, gloves, and mouthpieces, and docks foul points for low blows or headbutts

facts_and_myths.claim: A boxing referee must wait for a fighter to be knocked completely unconscious before stopping a fight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The referee's primary legal duty is preserving human life; they will call a Technical Knockout (TKO) whenever a fighter takes sustained unanswered blows.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Referees routinely consult the ringside physician between rounds to inspect severe facial cuts and eye swelling.

facts_and_myths.claim: Professional boxing referees wear surgical latex gloves inside the ring to protect against bloodborne pathogens.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Referees constantly touch bleeding facial lacerations and mouthpieces while separating fighters, making protective gloves mandatory.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Referees are often referred to by commentators as 'the third man in the ring'.

name: Sports Coach
visual_anchor: A head coach wearing a headset and team track jacket shouting strategic plays with a dry-erase tactical clipboard from the sidelines of an electric stadium game.
core_traits: Develops athletic strategies, player skills, team formations, and game plans for competitive sports teams
Conducts film breakdown sessions, scouting opposing teams to exploit tactical weaknesses
Manages player substitutions, timeouts, in-game tactical adjustments, and team morale
Coordinates with strength coaches, physical therapists, and athletic trainers to optimize conditioning

facts_and_myths.claim: Coaching effectiveness is determined solely by shouting loudly and yelling at players during games.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern sports coaching is heavily grounded in sports psychology, data analytics, biomechanics, and empathetic communication.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Top professional coaches spend hundreds of hours studying advanced statistical expected-value models.

facts_and_myths.claim: John Wooden led the UCLA Bruins to 10 NCAA national basketball championships in 12 years using his famous 'Pyramid of Success'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Considered one of the greatest coaches in sports history, Wooden emphasized character, fundamentals, and team unselfishness over winning.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: At the first practice of every season, Wooden famously taught his star players how to put on their socks and shoes properly to avoid blisters.

name: Martial Arts Master
visual_anchor: A martial arts master in a crisp black gi with an embroidered black belt executing a powerful side kick in a traditional wooden dojo under shoji screens.
core_traits: Teaches and preserves traditional martial arts disciplines: Karate, Judo, Taekwondo, Kung Fu, or Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu
Guides students through formal kata forms, controlled sparring (kumite), self-defense, and philosophy
Awards belt ranks from white belt to advanced black belt degrees (Dan ranks)
Emphasizes mental discipline, physical conditioning, humility, and respectful bowing etiquette

facts_and_myths.claim: A black belt in martial arts certifies that a person is an invincible, lethal fighting machine.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In traditional Japanese martial arts, a first-degree black belt (Shodan) simply signifies that the student has mastered the fundamental basics and is now ready to begin true learning.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The black belt is a beginning step in advanced study rather than a terminal finish line.

facts_and_myths.claim: Jigoro Kano founded Judo in 1882 based on the principle of using an opponent's own force and balance against them.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The word 'Judo' translates to 'the gentle way'; Kano removed lethal strikes from ancient jujutsu to create an Olympic sport centered on leverage and throws.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Kano invented the modern colored belt ranking system that is now used by martial arts across the world.

name: Architect
visual_anchor: An architect in stylish spectacles reviewing 3D architectural elevations and white scale physical building models on a drafting table in a glass-walled studio.
core_traits: Plans and designs the aesthetic form, spatial functionality, and spatial experience of buildings and complexes
Produces architectural blueprints, digital BIM models (Building Information Modeling), and physical scale models
Balances aesthetic vision with building codes, environmental sustainability, natural daylight, and accessibility
Coordinates with structural civil engineers, MEP consultants, and general contractors during construction

facts_and_myths.claim: Architects and structural engineers do the exact same job and calculate the same rebar formulas.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Architects design the spatial aesthetics, functional flow, and human interaction of spaces; structural engineers calculate the mathematical loads and steel beams that keep it standing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An architectural masterpiece is the result of a creative partnership between the architect's design and the engineer's calculations.

facts_and_myths.claim: Frank Lloyd Wright designed the iconic home 'Fallingwater' directly over an active waterfall in 1935.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rather than building facing the waterfall, Wright cantilevered reinforced concrete terraces directly over Bear Run stream so the owners would live with the waterfall.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fallingwater is celebrated as one of the greatest masterpieces of organic architecture in human history.

name: Librarian
visual_anchor: A knowledgeable librarian shelving leather-bound volumes between towering oak bookshelves in a majestic quiet public reading room illuminated by green banker lamps.
core_traits: Curates, organizes, catalogs, and provides public access to books, digital archives, and educational information
Utilizes classification cataloging systems: Dewey Decimal Classification and Library of Congress systems
Assists patrons with academic research queries, citation verification, and digital literacy instruction
Defends intellectual freedom, community literacy programs, and open access to knowledge

facts_and_myths.claim: Librarians spend their workday quietly reading novels at their desks and shushing patrons.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Professional librarians hold Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) degrees and manage complex digital databases, community technology, and archive acquisitions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern libraries offer 3D printers, business research databases, and community outreach programs.

facts_and_myths.claim: The ancient Great Library of Alexandria in Egypt aimed to acquire a copy of every single written book in the world.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Under the Ptolemaic dynasty, all ships entering Alexandria's harbor were required to surrender their scrolls to be copied and cataloged by scholars.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Head librarian Eratosthenes used the library's geometry scrolls to calculate the circumference of the Earth with astounding accuracy.

name: Museum Curator
visual_anchor: A museum curator wearing white conservation cotton gloves inspecting an ancient Egyptian bronze relic inside a climate-controlled glass vitrine display case.
core_traits: Acquires, cares for, authenticates, and organizes collections of historical artifacts, cultural relics, or fine artwork
Designs educational public exhibitions, gallery layouts, interpretive labels, and audio tours
Conducts historical research into artifact provenance, artist attribution, and cultural contexts
Ensures strict museum environmental standards: temperature, lux lighting levels, and humidity control

facts_and_myths.claim: Museum curators touch and clean priceless ancient oil paintings with ordinary tap water and sponges.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Curators and conservators use microscopic chemical solvents, purified saliva enzymes, and micro-suction tables to clean paintings without stripping original varnish.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Human saliva contains the enzyme amylase, which has historically been used as a gentle, non-destructive cleaning agent for delicate surfaces.

facts_and_myths.claim: Most major world museums display less than 10% of their total artifact collections to the public at any given time.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The vast majority of museum holdings are safely preserved in specialized underground climate-controlled storage vaults for research and rotation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The British Museum holds over 8 million artifacts, but can only display roughly 80,000 at a time.

name: High School Teacher
visual_anchor: An engaging high school teacher writing a physics equation on a green chalkboard in front of an attentive classroom of teenage students raising their hands.
core_traits: Instructs adolescent students in specialized academic subjects like mathematics, history, literature, or sciences
Prepares lesson plans, assesses student homework, grades examinations, and conducts parent-teacher conferences
Maintains classroom engagement and prepares students for standardized college entrance exams and careers
Fosters critical thinking, social development, and extracurricular student clubs

facts_and_myths.claim: Teachers only work 9 months out of the year and finish their work day when the 3:00 PM school bell rings.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Teachers spend dozens of unpaid hours every week grading essays, preparing lesson plans, attending faculty meetings, and taking summer continuing education credits.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Surveys show teachers work an average of 53 hours per week during the academic school year.

facts_and_myths.claim: The word 'pedagogy', referring to the art of teaching, comes from ancient Greece where enslaved guides walked children to school.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In ancient Athens, a 'paidagogos' was an attendant entrusted with leading boys to and from school and teaching them manners along the way.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over centuries, the term evolved into the academic science of educational teaching methods.

name: University Professor
visual_anchor: A distinguished university professor in a tweed blazer lecturing from an oak lectern inside a tiered amphitheater lecture hall to hundreds of university students.
core_traits: Conducts advanced scholarly research, publishes peer-reviewed journal papers, and lectures undergraduate/graduate students
Mentors doctoral Ph.D. candidates, supervises master's dissertations, and serves on academic defense panels
Secures external research grants from scientific foundations, corporations, and government agencies
Attains academic tenure through years of peer-reviewed publication, teaching excellence, and university service

facts_and_myths.claim: The primary job duty of a research university professor is spending 40 hours a week giving classroom lectures.
facts_and_myths.explanation: At major research universities, professors spend the majority of their time running research laboratories, writing peer-reviewed papers, and applying for grants.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The academic phrase 'publish or perish' reflects the relentless pressure to publish original discoveries in respected journals.

facts_and_myths.claim: The University of Bologna in Italy, founded in 1088, is the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bologna established the concept of university degrees, academic faculties, and mutual student-teacher guild contracts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The academic graduation cap and gown trace their roots directly to medieval clerical robes worn by Bologna and Oxford scholars.

name: School Principal
visual_anchor: A confident school principal in a business suit walking down a vibrant school hallway greeting students and high-fiving teachers near classroom lockers.
core_traits: Serves as the educational leader and administrative director of an elementary, middle, or high school
Oversees school budgeting, faculty hiring, teacher evaluations, and campus safety protocols
Maintains school disciplinary standards, student counseling programs, and parent community relations
Implements district academic standards and coordinates state educational compliance audits

facts_and_myths.claim: The school principal's job is exclusively disciplining misbehaving students who get sent to the office.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Modern principals are instructional leaders who coach teachers, manage multi-million dollar school budgets, and foster school culture.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Principals spend significant time analyzing state test data trends to improve reading and math curricula across the entire school.

facts_and_myths.claim: The title 'principal' originally was an adjective modifying 'teacher' - meaning the 'principal teacher' of the school.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 19th-century common schools, the lead teacher assumed administrative responsibilities while still teaching classes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over time, administrative demands grew into a dedicated full-time leadership position and the noun 'principal' stuck.

name: Kindergarten Teacher
visual_anchor: A warm kindergarten teacher seated on a tiny wooden chair reading a picture book aloud to a circle of five-year-olds on an alphabet rug in a colorful classroom.
core_traits: Introduces early developmental learners to foundational reading literacy, numeracy, and social cooperation
Fosters motor skills through structured play, finger-painting, building blocks, and music games
Establishes daily behavioral classroom routines: circle time, sharing, active listening, and recess safety
Identifies early speech, hearing, and cognitive developmental delays for early childhood intervention

facts_and_myths.claim: Kindergarten is merely glorified babysitting where children do not learn any academic skills.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Early childhood education builds foundational phonemic awareness, number sense, and executive function that statistically predict lifelong academic success.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Brain development between ages 3 and 5 forms neural pathways faster than at any other point in human life.

facts_and_myths.claim: The word 'Kindergarten' was coined in Germany in 1837 by educator Friedrich Froebel, meaning 'children's garden'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Froebel believed young children should be nurtured and tended gently like young plants in a garden rather than drilled in strict rote memorization.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Froebel also invented the first educational toys, called 'Froebel Gifts', which included geometric wooden blocks that inspired architect Frank Lloyd Wright.

name: Judge
visual_anchor: A dignified judge in black judicial robes striking a polished wooden gavel on an elevated mahogany bench inside a stately wood-paneled courtroom.
core_traits: Presides over legal proceedings in courts of law, ensuring fair and impartial constitutional justice
Rules on legal motions, admissibility of evidence, jury instructions, and objections by attorneys
Delivers verdicts in bench trials and pronounces formal legal sentences in criminal convictions
Appointed or elected to interpret statutory law, judicial precedents, and constitutional protections

facts_and_myths.claim: Judges in modern British and Commonwealth courts still wear powdered white horsehair wigs in civil trials.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 2008, the UK Judicial Office abolished horsehair wigs for all civil, family, and Supreme Court hearings, retaining them only in traditional criminal trials.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Traditional horsehair wigs date back to the 17th century when King Charles II popularized them.

facts_and_myths.claim: The wooden gavel was originally used by American presiding officers in Congress before becoming a courtroom symbol.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Vice President John Adams struck an ivory gavel in the first U.S. Senate meeting in 1789 to bring legislators to order.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: British court judges do not use gavels; gavels are primarily used in American and international tribunals.

name: Lawyer
visual_anchor: A sharp attorney in a tailored dark suit standing at the podium passionately presenting cross-examination arguments before a courtroom jury.
core_traits: Licensed legal practitioner who advises clients, drafts legal documents, and advocates cases in court
Conducts legal research into statutes, case law precedents, and evidentiary discovery
Drafts contracts, corporate mergers, wills, and criminal defense motions
Admitted to the legal bar after completing law school (Juris Doctor) and passing the bar examination

facts_and_myths.claim: Lawyers spend 90% of their working career pacing theatrically in front of a jury in dramatic courtroom trials.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Over 95% of criminal and civil cases settle before ever reaching trial; most lawyers spend their careers reviewing documents, drafting contracts, and negotiating settlements.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many transactional corporate lawyers never step foot inside a courtroom throughout their entire career.

facts_and_myths.claim: The attorney-client privilege is one of the oldest recognized legal confidentiality protections in Anglo-American law.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dating back to the reign of Queen Elizabeth I in 1577, the rule guarantees that communications between client and lawyer cannot be disclosed without client consent.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The privilege encourages clients to be completely candid with their legal counsel so they can receive competent representation.

name: Diplomat
visual_anchor: A poised diplomat in formal business attire shaking hands with a foreign dignitary before bilateral nation flags inside an ornate embassy conference salon.
core_traits: Appointed government official who represents their nation's foreign policy and international relations abroad
Negotiates bilateral treaties, trade agreements, peace accords, and consular affairs in foreign embassies
Maintains diplomatic communication channels during international crises and armed conflicts
Protected internationally under the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations

facts_and_myths.claim: Foreign embassies are legally sovereign soil belonging physically to the foreign country, outside the host nation's borders.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The land remains part of the host country, but under the Vienna Convention, embassy premises are granted 'inviolability' - host police cannot enter without permission.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This inviolability ensures nations can conduct confidential diplomacy without fear of local police intrusion.

facts_and_myths.claim: Diplomats carry special black or red 'Diplomatic Passports' granting them diplomatic immunity from local prosecution.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Diplomatic immunity protects envoys from political harassment or arbitrary arrest by foreign host governments during international tensions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: However, if a diplomat commits a serious crime, the sending state can waive immunity or the host nation can expel them as 'persona non grata'.

name: News Anchor
visual_anchor: A poised news anchor with an earpiece sitting behind a curved studio glass desk reading breaking international news from a teleprompter facing studio cameras.
core_traits: Presents live television or digital news broadcasts, introducing field reporter packages and interviewing experts
Reads scripted breaking news stories smoothly from automated camera-mounted teleprompters
Listens to real-time director cues and timing adjustments through an in-ear monitor (IFB earpiece)
Adheres to journalistic standards of objectivity, fact-checking, and news verification

facts_and_myths.claim: News anchors write all their own breaking stories live while on air without relying on newsroom staff.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Anchors are supported by a massive newsroom team of producers, researchers, video editors, and field correspondents feeding facts and scripts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: However, during unexpected live breaking news events, anchors must ad-lib and conduct interviews unscripted for hours.

facts_and_myths.claim: Legendary CBS anchor Walter Cronkite was once voted 'the most trusted man in America' in nationwide opinion polls.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cronkite anchored the CBS Evening News from 1962 to 1981, guiding the nation through the JFK assassination, the Moon landing, and Vietnam.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Cronkite ended his broadcasts with his iconic sign-off catchphrase: 'And that's the way it is.'

name: War Correspondent
visual_anchor: A courageous war correspondent in a blue ballistic flak vest clearly marked 'PRESS' and a combat helmet reporting into a microphone amid rubble in a war zone.
core_traits: Investigative journalist who reports on armed conflicts, civil wars, and humanitarian crises directly from frontline combat zones
Wears prominent blue body armor and ballistic helmets emblazoned with large white 'PRESS' lettering
Transmits live eyewitness reports, combat footage, and civilian interviews via portable BGAN satellite terminals
Operates under international humanitarian law as protected non-combatants under the Geneva Conventions

facts_and_myths.claim: War correspondents are armed with military rifles to engage in direct combat alongside the soldiers they cover.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Carrying weapons forfeits non-combatant status under the Geneva Conventions; journalists must remain unarmed neutral observers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bearing arms would make the journalist a lawful military target and endanger other reporters.

facts_and_myths.claim: Renowned World War II correspondent Ernie Pyle lived directly alongside frontline infantry soldiers in European trenches.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pyle won a Pulitzer Prize in 1944 for his poignant columns describing the daily hardships of common infantry soldiers ('dogfaces') before being killed by machine-gun fire in Okinawa in 1945.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pyle was so beloved by soldiers that President Truman paid tribute to him as an essential voice of the American GI.
